title: Terence Stamp: A Group of Film Scripts from the 1960s and 1970s including Blue, Poor Cow, and Modesty Blaise, 1960s and 1970s, Qty
description: The Terence Stamp Collection Terence Stamp: A Group of Film Scripts from the 1960s and 1970s including Blue, Poor Cow, and Modesty Blaise , 1960s and 1970s, Comprising: 'Poor Cow', screenplay by Nell Dunn, dated 'February 1967', bound in burgundy paper covers, with revision pages on various coloured papers and pagination marked '75' to the upper right; 'Blue', screenplay by Meade Roberts and Ronald M. Cohen, dated '28 June 1967', directed by Silvio Narizzano, inscribed by Terence Stamp to the upper right and extensively annotated, incorporating green revision pages; 'The Mind of Mr. Soames', screenplay by Stanley Mann and John Hale, adapted from the novel by Charles Eric Maine, revised draft dated '2 January 1969', inscribed by Terence Stamp to the upper right, with amendments on pages of varying colours; 'A Season in Hell', two versions, screenplay by Raffaele La Capria and Nelo Risi; 'The Thief of Baghdad', original screenplay by A. J. Carothers, adapted by Andrew Birkin, dated '3 March 1978', bound in green covers with metal binding, accompanied by a group of stills from the set; 'Together?' (originally titled 'Amo non amo' or 'I Love You, I Love You Not'), '1979' Italian romantic drama directed by Armenia Balducci; and 'Modesty Blaise', revised script dated '25 June 1965', bound in light blue covers with metal binding clips, heavily annotated, with pagination marked '77' and inscription to the upper right of the cover page, together with a poster; accompanied by a page of costume drawings and watercolour detailing, signed 'Malak Khazai' to the lower left corner; together with various production stills and scripts, (Qty)

title: 1925 Bentley 3-Litre Boat-Tail Tourer Chassis no. 954 Engine no. 879
description: 1925 Bentley 3-Litre Boat-Tail Tourer Registration no. KU 5705 Chassis no. 954 Engine no. 879 • Originally bodied by Vanden Plas as a 4/5-seat tourer • Restored in the 2000s • Present ownership since circa 2016 • Benefiting from recent servicing With characteristic humility, Walter Owen Bentley ('W O') was constantly amazed by the enthusiasm of later generations for the products of Bentley Motors Limited, and it is testimony to the soundness of his engineering design skills that so many of his products have survived. From the humblest of beginnings in a mews garage off Baker Street, London in 1919 the Bentley rapidly achieved fame as an exciting fast touring car, well able to compete with the best of European and American sports cars in the tough world of motor sport in the 1920s. Bentley's domination at Le Mans in 1924, 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 is legendary, and one can only admire the Herculean efforts of such giants as Woolf Barnato, Jack Dunfee, Tim Birkin and Sammy Davis, consistently wrestling the British Racing Green sports cars to victory. W O Bentley had proudly unveiled the new 3-litre car bearing his name on Stand 126 at the 1919 Olympia Motor Exhibition, the prototype engine having fired up for the first time just a few weeks earlier. Bentley's four-cylinder 'fixed head' engine incorporated a single overhead camshaft, four-valves per cylinder and a bore/stroke of 80x149mm. Twin ML magnetos provided the ignition, and power was transmitted via a four-speed gearbox with right-hand change. The pressed-steel chassis started off with a wheelbase of 9' 9½", then adopted dimensions of 10' 10" ('Long Standard') in 1923, the shorter frame being reserved for the TT Replica and subsequent Speed Model. Rear wheel brakes only were employed up to 1924 when four-wheel Perrot-type brakes were introduced. In only mildly developed form, this was the model that was to become a legend in motor racing history and which, with its leather-strapped bonnet, classical radiator design and British Racing Green livery, has become the archetypal Vintage sports car. Early success in the 1922 Isle of Man Tourist Trophy, when Bentleys finished second, fourth, and fifth to take the Team Prize, led to the introduction of the TT Replica (later known as the Speed Model and identified by the Red Label on its radiator) on the existing 9' 9½" wheelbase, Short Standard chassis. Bentley had made approximately 1,600 3-Litre models by the time production ceased in 1929, the majority of which was bodied by Vanden Plas with either open tourer or saloon coachwork. Dr Clare Hay's authoritative work, Bentley, The Vintage Years , records the fact that Long Standard chassis number '954' was issued with the registration number 'KU 5705' in March 1925. The 3-Litre was supplied new to a Miss Frances Eliza Ingleby (later Mrs J E Hamilton) and bodied by Vanden Plas as a 4/5-seat Tourer. Some time later, 'KU 5705' was damaged in an accident and scrapped, its chassis being used to repair another damaged 3-Litre, 'YX 5984' (chassis number 'DN1729'). However, it is believed that part of chassis '954' was stored and later used as the basis of the resurrected 'KU 5705' (a chassis stamping stated as proof). When the Bentley was offered for sale at a UK auction in October 2008, it came with a V5C registration document issued to chassis '954' for the UK registration number, 'KU 5705'. At that time the car was said to have recently benefited from a painstaking restoration, including a new radiator. Its chassis was described as a shortened 'Red Label'-style on the 9ft 9½" wheelbase, while the boat-tail body was said to have been 'acquired from another 3-Litre at enormous expense'. The engine currently fitted to 'KU 5705' began life in 'EC 5874' (chassis '876'), which served as a fire tender at Brooklands from around 1934 until 1939. Renowned Bentley specialist Russell 'Rusty' Turner supplied the aluminium rear axle. The 2008 auction catalogue stated that the car was still being run-in having covered only some 300-or-so miles since the rebuild. The Bentley was described by the vendor as in 'very good overall' condition. Our vendor purchased 'KU 5705' circa 10 years ago from The School Garage in Whaley Bridge, Derbyshire. She had gone there to purchase an Alvis but ended up buying the Bentley as well! It is offered for sale today benefiting from recent servicing by a local specialist.

title: 1949 Bentley Mark VI B80 'Speed 8' Special by Racing Green Engineering Chassis no. B36EY Engine no. B18E (see text)
description: 1949 Bentley Mark VI B80 'Speed 8' Special by Racing Green Engineering Registration no. not UK registered Chassis no. B36EY Engine no. B18E (see text) • Completed circa 2010 • Believed 1,078 miles since completion • Rolls-Royce B80 6.0-litre straight-eight engine • Owned for over 10 years This spectacular Bentley Special is the creation of the renowned Racing Green Engineering Limited, a company with many years experience in the building of re-creations and specials on Bentley and other high quality chassis. Their 'Speed 8' recalls Bentley's 6½-Litre model, known to be W O Bentley's favourite design, which in Speed Six form won the Le Mans 24-Hour Race in Hours in 1929 and 1930 with 'Bentley Boys' 'Tim' Birkin, Glen Kidston and Woolf Barnato, establishing itself as one of the most iconic racing cars of its day. According to Racing Green: "The coachwork of the Speed 8 follows the construction of the original Le Mans cars with an ash frame panelled with aluminium and fabric covered to the chosen colour of the car. A new aluminium instrument panel is fitted incorporating high quality reproductions of the original instruments. The interior is finished in Connolly leather and leather bound carpets. The fold flat windscreen has aero screens of the type that can be used in the normal scuttle position or as draught deflectors alongside the windscreen. It is fitted with hood tonneau cover and hood bag. These cars have at their heart the B Series straight 8 engines, fitted with 4 SU Carburettors and a choice of rear axle ratios. Electrics have been upgraded to meet the demands of modern motoring and rally use, The robust MK6 chassis is used as the basis of the car." This particular car is based on a modified Bentley Mark VI chassis, number 'B36EY', which started life in 1949 as a 'standard steel' model delivered new to one C Cunnington in the UK. The original UK registration was 'KLP 601'. This leviathan is powered by a 6.0-litre Rolls-Royce B80 straight-eight engine, which breathes via a quartet of SU carburettors mounted on a balanced and polished aluminium inlet manifold. This mighty power unit belongs to the B-series of engines developed towards the end of WW2 for military and commercial purposes. A derivative found its way into the ultra-rare Phantom IV. Maximum power output of a standard B80 was around 160bhp at a mere 3,750rpm. This car's engine has been stamped with the number ('B18E') of the original six-cylinder Bentley power unit. This Bentley Special has been built in the ever-popular 'Le Mans' style, featuring a new replica body in aluminium to broadly Speed Six specifications. The build was finished around 2010, and the current odometer reading of 1,078 miles is assumed to be the distance covered since its completion. On file is an Oldtimertaxatie Valuation Report, compiled on the vendor's behalf in April 2024, which describes the chassis as 'beautifully restored, in as new condition with hardly any trace of use'. The body likewise was found to be in excellent condition according to the report, as was the newly reupholstered red leather interior. The engine bay is clean, with only slight traces of use, while the engine itself has been rebuilt to Racing Green specifications. The Mark VI suspension, four-wheel hydraulic brakes and rewired electrics were all found to be in similarly excellent condition. The valuation report concludes that the car looks in as new condition. Offered with European registration papers and a copy of a UK V5. Please note that this vehicle is from outside the UK. Our customs agents, CARS UK, will manage all post sale customs administration. A fee of £350+VAT will be charged on the buyer's invoice to administer both import or export customs movements. If the buyer also chooses to ship with CARS UK, this will be quoted separately. If this vehicle is to remain in the UK, it will be subject to Import VAT at the reduced rate of 5% on the hammer price. This vehicle will not be available for immediate collection after the sale and will only be released on completion of customs clearance formalities. If you have any questions regarding customs clearance, please contact the Bonhams Motorcar Department.

title: 1933 MG Magnette K3 Supercharged Sports-Racing Two-Seater Chassis no. K3003 (see text) Engine no. R772 AC
description: 1933 MG Magnette K3 Supercharged Sports-Racing Two-Seater Registration no. JB1475 Chassis no. K3003 (see text) Engine no. R772 AC • Credited with use by Tazio Nuvolari, Captain George Eyston, • Credited with winning the 1933 RAC Tourist Trophy at Ards and 1100cc class 1933 Mille Miglia Here we offer this highly significant and important example of the MG K3 breed, the 1100cc supercharged cars from Abingdon-on-Thames which did so much to enhance the prestige of the British motor industry. The K3 offered here spent many years on display in the Fremantle and York Motor Museums, Western Australia, and is considered from available evidence to be the car handled by the legendary Italian superstar driver Tazio Nuvolari in winning the greatest British sports car race of the era – the RAC Tourist Trophy on the Ards circuit in Ulster, the Mille Miglia class win and results at Brooklands and Shelsley Walsh. This car's two race wins in Ulster and Italy marked the high point of MG in international competition, not bettered by a British car until the rise of Jaguar in the post-war years. The legendary K3 is the most sought after MG of the pre-war era. The car now known simply as a K3 by the MG fraternity is powered by a supercharged 1,087cc overhead camshaft six-cylinder engine with cross-flow cylinder head. The high-boost blower, fed by a single SU carburettor, is mounted in front of the radiator and the combination could generate in excess of 120bhp at 6500rpm in factory tune. The K3 features a four-speed ENV Wilson Pre-Selector transmission, semi-elliptic springs and live axles. This innovative gearbox enables fast gear changes on demanding road courses. The cable operated drum brakes are 13-inch magnesium with bolted-in liners. Steering is split-track operated by the unique K3 Bishop-cam steering box. Double acting André shock absorbers are fitted, two at the front and four at the rear. The complete package marked a great step forward in British sports/racing car design and made the K3 competitive with the best small sports/racing cars of the era from France and Italy. Two prototypes (K3751 and K3752) were constructed and tested, followed by three team cars for the MG team to race in the 1933 Mille Miglia. Their chassis were numbered from 3001-3003. The car we offer here features the 'Mille Miglia' body with trademark gutter around the cabin area which was added to the design after testing a prototype in Italy. It also has twin aero screens, dashboard-mounted Kigas to assist starting, leather bonnet straps, and spare wheel. The interior is trimmed in green leather, with a full complement of instruments. The car sits on four triple-laced wire wheels retained by knock-off spinners. Finally, it is equipped with an enormous slab-tank fuel tank with twin quick-filler caps. The first chapter in the story of the K3s is of their appearance as a team contesting the ultimate sports car racing challenge of the day, the 1933 Mille Miglia (1,000-mile) round-Italy road race. This event had been dominated by Italian marques. The challenge to Italian supremacy was underwritten by the English aristocrat and frontline racing driver, Earl Howe, who convinced Sir William Morris that MG could create a car which would be highly competitive in this international arena. Lt. Col. John Thornley – postwar Director and General Manager of MG – wrote of the K3 in 1950 when recollecting the race: "The members of the team, Earl Howe, Sir Henry Birkin, Captain Eyston, Bernard Rubin, Count 'Johnny' Lurani...and Hugh Hamilton...tested the prototype in Italy in January....Birkin (broke) the class record at the first control, 220 miles, by 25 minutes, then had to retire with a burnt exhaust valve...Birkin averaged 87.95mph for the 130 miles from Brescia to Bologna, and in places all three cars had exceeded 110mph. This – let us remind ourselves – was 1933; the race was 1,000 miles; the engines were less than 1.1-litres. With Birkin out, Eyston and Lurani took the class lead and continued the headlong dash through the rest of the day and most of the following night, with Howe and Hamilton in second place. As, by shortly after half distance, both cars had overtaken all the runners in the smaller classes, the two MGs were the first cars on the course and were, in fact, the first cars to reach Brescia again and the finish. This they did after 18 hours of the hardest possible driving, with but 90 seconds between them, having averaged 56.9 and 56.82mph respectively..." This underlines the tremendously usable character of these great little supercharged six-cylinder-engined MGs although Thornley did go on to observe that "...speeds would have been much higher had it not been for constant stops to change plugs. Eyston and Lurani fitted 157 new sparking plugs in the course of the 1,000 miles....sufficient oil had to be fed to the (*Powerplus) supercharger to keep it happy under high-speed, full-throttle conditions, and this proved excessive on over-run...the MGs received the Team Prize (and) by the time the Italian dust settled, series production of the K3 was under way...four were entered for the JCC International Trophy (at Brooklands)...second, third and fourth places at speeds for the 260 miles in excess of 80mph...in August, Whitney Straight scored a dramatic win over a flock of single-seat Maseratis in the Coppa Acerbo at Pescara; a fortnight later Nuvolari won the RAC Ulster TT; a fortnight later still E.R. Hall came first in the BRDC 500-mile race at Brooklands and in the following month Whitney Straight captured the Brooklands Mountain lap record". The much-publicised victory at the RAC Tourist Trophy on the Ards circuit in Ulster was a tribute to the diminutive, then 40-year old, Nuvolari's transcendent skills but also to the qualities of the MG K3 which withstood the immense stresses to which he subjected it. The Magnette's average speed for the race was 78.65mph, well over 4mph faster than the best car in the same class the previous year. This great victory, with Hugh Hamilton's MG finishing a very close second – established the MG K3 Magnette's place in British motor racing history. During this particular car's long preservation at the Fremantle and York Motor Museums, historian Graeme Cocks produced a lavish and very well-received book on the 1933 K3 team cars, 'The Mighty MG Magnettes of 33', sub-titled 'The Cars, the Drivers, The Mystery' which references the long discussion about the fate of what has become the most successful and storied K3. It is accepted from contemporary works records that MG K3 chassis 'K3003' had been driven by Captain George Eyston/Count Giovanni Lurani to win the 1100cc class in the Mille Miglia so narrowly from team-mates Earl Howe/Hugh Hamilton in K3 '3001'. The victorious 'K3003' was then recorded as having been the outright-winning Nuvolari/Hounslow mount in the Ards TT, for which it was fitted with a different lightweight body to meet RAC regulations. After the Nuvolari victory in the prestigious RAC Tourist Trophy race, it spent some months on an MG dealer tour for sales-promotional display. It was lightly damaged in an accident apparently en route to the Shelsley Walsh hill-climb. At about this time, Theodore Fork from Germany agreed to buy K3003 if it were returned to 1933 Mille Miglia specification so he could compete in the 1934 event. The British MG historian and former MG employee, Mike Allison, was told by the head of the Competition Department at that time, Reg Jackson, that as K3003 was on a promotional tour and unavailable, the MG engineer HN Charles instructed that a new car be built up and fitted with an original Mille Miglia body. This new car was then given the identity of K3003 and sent to Herr Fork in Germany. The car passed to Herr Fork for 1934 had not used the actual Eyston/Nuvolari chassis at all, but "a better" replacement using the road 'identity' (presumably registration 'JB 1475') of the original. Reg Jackson maintained that the Fork sale – in which the customer had insisted upon acquiring "the Nuvolari car" - had actually become "a bit of a fiddle". As quoted by author Graeme Cocks, Mike Allison wrote a statement in 2010 confirming the elements of a conversation with Mr Jackson who had told him: "The car after the TT was sent on a round of dealers. I had it cleaned a bit, took out the carburettor needle, although actually it was a standard RM8, and removed the rotor arm: we didn't want any of the clowns giving driving tests of the car...Anyway off the car went, in October for a three month trip around the country. I then got a message that someone in Germany wanted that car returned to Mille Miglia trim for him to use in the '34 race in April. In the event, what with transport difficulties and so forth, I found the car wasn't due back in Abingdon until February at the earliest. I appealed to HN (Hubert Noel Charles), and he just said 'Build him another car'. So we did just that using all new chassis and running gear, built a new engine up, and fitted one of the Mille Miglia bodies. It was given the road identity of the original car, which George (Eyston) had driven in the '33 race, and it was despatched to Jack Woodhouse about the time the Nuvolari car came back to Abingdon, but well in time for this guy Fork to drive in the '34 race." Mr Jackson's memory was that the original car was pirated for parts at the factory in 1937 and was eventually sold. He told Mike Allison that the original number had been partly ground down (to delete the zeros on the chassis) giving the new identity K33. In 1938, one Ronald Victor Robinson of Sandsend bought a K3 – with the non-standard-style chassis number 'K33', strongly suggesting that two zeros had been filed off and it was the car mentioned by Reg Jackson. The car came with bodies in both two-seat and ex-Goldie Gardner single-seat form - from famed London sports car and aircraft dealer, Jack Bartlett. Australian author Graeme Cocks explains: "The chassis was identified as K33 which was atypical of the numbering system used by the MG Car Company. The original chassis number (K3003) was, according to Jacko, on the car which was sent to Germany, so a new identity would have had to have been created for the car in England. It was a simple matter to remove a couple of numbers from the dumb iron - K3003 became K33". Just postwar, Robinson sold the car to Toulmin Motors of Hanworth, Middlesex. Unable to find a buyer for it in single-seat form, they converted the car to two-seat sports configuration with HRG aerodynamic bodywork and advertised the result for sale in 'Motor Sport' magazine, December, 1950 issue. The car remained road taxed in the UK until July 1959 and was subsequently retrieved from a scrapyard by Tom Davis of Toulmin Motors. MG enthusiast Mike Ellman Brown acquired it and set about the task of establishing exactly what he had in his garage. He had a Police forensic examiner investigate its partially ground-off original frame stamping. Mr Ellman Brown stated that the tests concluded the stamp read 'K3003'. In 1966, he sold the car to Dr Stuart Milton, from whose estate it passed in early 1972 to Philip Bayne-Powell. It presented a formidable restoration project, but Mr Bayne-Powell had it running by 1975 when Captain George Eyston – the renowned former MG team member who became the Land Speed record-breaking 'Fastest Man on Earth' and was universally respected and popular - drove it at a Brands Hatch MG Car Club meeting. As Graeme Cocks wrote: "Despite the question marks raised by doubters, Philip Bayne-Powell embarked on a five-year career of historic motor racing...The car enjoyed several race wins and was always competitive...". In 1984, it was sold to British-born Australian businessman, entrepreneur and fine car enthusiast, Peter Briggs, for his developing York Motor Museum. The price paid was £45,000 and this striking MG finally arrived in Western Australia in 1986. Mr Briggs then had Acting Senior Sergeant R.A.Warburton of the Western Australia Police Ballistic Section apply the latest available detection technology to establish what original chassis number had been stamped into the K3 chassis frame's front dumb-iron. The officer's report of his three-hour forensic test, dated March 22, 1994 reported that "The details restored are as follows: 'k3-0-3" appearing "...to be a four (4) letter/number sequence". Content with this finding, Mr Briggs felt fully justified in presenting this car as the restored version of the original Eyston Mille Miglia/Nuvolari Ards TT K3. He raced it hard in Australian and New Zealand historic events, displayed it in the Fremantle Motor Museum 2002-2007, and had it restored and maintained by the respected specialist, John Hunting. During restoration, Mr Hunting dismantled the car and carefully photographed the chassis and running gear. He identified elements of the chassis which conformed with the other very early production team cars and supported the conclusion that, on the balance of all the historical and physical evidence, the car was indeed 1933 team car K3003. It is perhaps understandable that the K3 restored by Philip Bayne-Powell has been the subject of a great deal of debate. K3003 was, after all, the most successful MG in international motor sport during the 1930s and the car which typified the spirit of MG and its sports/racing reputation. For decades its history has been subject to much study and speculation by many in the MG movement. Hard evidence supports the conclusion that this is indeed the immensely successful 1933 Nuvolari/Eyston/Lurani car. • The rolling chassis has the attributes of the very first K3s produced and two forensic chassis-stamp examinations support the belief that the frame is indeed that of K3003. • The historical evidence provides a plausible timeline from 1933 to its Bayne-Powell restoration. • The car has been faithfully restored and genuine, original components have been documented as part of the process. Mr Briggs shipped the car to Italy for the 2013 Mille Miglia retro event, starting as No 65 with wife Robin as his intrepid passenger. Today the car is offered here, fresh from running at the Goodwood Festival of Speed where it ran on the hillclimb as one of the feature cars celebrating the Centenary of the MG Car Company. It is sold with several spares including the early spec tailshaft (which helps identify it as one of the early team cars), supercharger cover etc. As an early 1933 MG K3 with team car pedigree and a fascinating history, we recommend it for serious consideration as an immensely useable and enjoyable Post-Vintage Thoroughbred competition car linked to two of the most important race accomplishments by a British team and a British car, and not least when driven by a future 'Fastest Man on Earth' and by Italy's 'Greatest Racing Driver of All Time'. Please note that this vehicle is from outside the UK. Our customs agents, CARS UK, will manage all post sale customs administration. A fee of £350+VAT will be charged on the buyer's invoice to administer both import or export customs movements. If the buyer also chooses to ship with CARS UK, this will be quoted separately. If this vehicle is to remain in the UK, it will be subject to Import VAT at the reduced rate of 5% on the hammer price. This vehicle will not be available for immediate collection after the sale and will only be released on completion of customs clearance formalities. If you have any questions regarding customs clearance, please contact the Bonhams Motorcar Department.

title: 1927 Bentley 3-Litre Sports Project Chassis no. TN1566 Engine no. TN1567
description: 1927 Bentley 3-Litre Sports Project Registration no. YF 2654 Chassis no. TN1566 Engine no. TN1567 • Originally an Offord-bodied coupé • Matching chassis and engine • Family owned since March 1957 • Garaged unused for some 50-plus years • 'Barn find' offered for restoration With characteristic humility 'W O' was constantly amazed by the enthusiasm of later generations for the products of Bentley Motors Limited, and it is testimony to the soundness of his engineering design skills that so many of his products have survived. From the humblest of beginnings in a mews garage off Baker Street, London in 1919 the Bentley rapidly achieved fame as an exciting fast touring car, well able to compete with the best of European and American sports cars in the tough world of motor sport in the 1920s. Bentley's domination at Le Mans in 1924, 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 is legendary, and one can only admire the Herculean efforts of such giants as Woolf Barnato, Jack Dunfee, Tim Birkin and Sammy Davis, consistently wrestling the British Racing Green sports cars to victory. W O Bentley proudly unveiled the new 3-litre car bearing his name on Stand 126 at the 1919 Olympia Motor Exhibition, the prototype engine having fired up for the first time just a few weeks earlier. Bentley's four-cylinder 'fixed head' engine incorporated a single overhead camshaft, four-valves per cylinder and a bore/stroke of 80x149mm. Twin ML magnetos provided the ignition and power was transmitted via a four-speed gearbox with right-hand change. The pressed-steel chassis started off with a wheelbase of 9' 9½", then adopted dimensions of 10' 10" ('Standard Long') in 1923, the shorter frame being reserved for the TT Replica and subsequent Speed Model. Rear wheel brakes only were employed up to 1924 when four-wheel Perrot-type brakes were introduced. In only mildly developed form, this was the model that was to become a legend in motor racing history and which, with its leather-strapped bonnet, classical radiator design and British Racing Green livery, has become the archetypal Vintage sports car. Early success in the 1922 Isle of Man Tourist Trophy, when Bentleys finished second, fourth, and fifth to take the Team Prize, led to the introduction of the TT Replica (later known as the Speed Model and identified by the Red Label on its radiator ) on the existing 9' 9½" wheelbase, short standard chassis. Bentley had made approximately 1,600 3-Litre models when production ceased in 1929, the majority of which were bodied by Vanden Plas with either open tourer or saloon coachwork. Dr Clare Hay's authoritative work, Bentley, The Vintage Years , records the fact that chassis number 'TN1566' (with engine number '1567') was completed in April 1927 on the long standard 10' 10" wheelbase chassis with coupé coachwork by Offord. Hay records that 'TN1567' was first owned by one W A Thompson and registered as 'YF 2654', noting: "Now 2 seater on 9' 0" wheelbase." It is not known when this modification was carried out. The next ownership record we have is an old-style buff logbook issued on 1st June 1950 listing four owners: Arthur Ratcliffe Ainsworth of Dorking; A B B Woodburn of Bolesworth; Bursledon Autos of Sholing; and one Miss Mary Louisa White, BSc, who registered the Bentley on 2nd March 1957. Miss White appears to have been a most enthusiastic owner, a view supported by the numerous Bentley Drivers Club membership cards on file, mostly dating from the late 1950s to the mid 1970s, while there are also some spectator's passes, an RAC membership card and a VCC official's badge. According to the deceased's family, Miss Mary Louisa White passed away in 2005 and was the last known person to drive the Bentley in the late 50s or early 60s. 'YF 2654' was then left to Miss Nicola White, (the last recorded keepers' niece) along with the property where the Bentley was kept. Miss Nicola White passed away in July 2023. Additional documentation includes assorted correspondence, sundry bills, insurance paperwork, a later buff logbook (1963), an old-style V5 registration document, and four MoT certificates, the most recent of which was issued in 1964. The most recent tax discs on file date from the 1960s, so it seems reasonable to conclude that the Bentley was taken off the road sometime towards the end of that decade. It has remained in the owner's garage ever since, concealed beneath a variety of non-Bentley-related clutter, and is presented in 'barn find' condition, ripe for sympathetic restoration. Sold strictly as viewed, 'YF 2654' represents a wonderful opportunity to bring a long-forgotten 'W O' Bentley back to life.

title: 1933 Maserati Tipo 8C-3000 Biposto Engine no. 3004
description: 1933 Maserati Tipo 8C-3000 Biposto Engine no. 3004 • Formerly part of the Willem van Huystee Collection • Awesome, supercharged road-going Grand Prix car • Proven in road tours and competitions • Mechanically sorted by expert Chris Leydon • Road registered in the Netherlands The Maserati brothers had developed their powerful new Tipo 8C 3.0-litre straight-eight supercharged engine in 1932. It powered low-slung offset two-seater cars before chassis '3005' became the first pure central-seat monoposto, founding the long line of customer Grand Prix production cars which cemented Maserati's reputation through the mid-1930s and culminated in their great post-war classic: the highly-prized Maserati 250F. What survivors there were of the 1933 Maserati 8Cs seem to have ended up in the USA after WW2. As far as can been ascertained, the first two 3-litre cars, '3001' and '3002', were in the USA by the early 1960s, where they were discovered by long time car sleuth, collector and historian Richard 'Dick' Merritt in two separate finds, together with numerous Maserati components, which included crankcase '3004'. These would eventually pass to noted British Maserati enthusiast Cameron Miller, who sold one to the late Bob Sutherland, founder of the Colorado Grand, and elected to keep the ex-Birkin car, '3002'. At this point, all were sent to expert Maserati restorer Peter Shaw to return them to the road. The surviving chassis '3001' and '3002' took priority, while Shaw himself negotiated the purchase of the crankcase '3004'. While Shaw was busy restoring those cars, a chance offering of a Maserati rear axle from John Hewitt began the revival of this car. The axle had been retrieved from the garages of Roland Dutt, a noted former owner of '3001', and was numbered '3004'. Over the course of the ensuing years, Shaw was also able to source a period, though slightly earlier, gearbox (number '26') and the project began to take shape. Since the British Vintage Sports Car Club's racing regulations at this time stipulated a minimum 'three of five' major component rule, this would provide him with a car that he could campaign/race. With his unique experience and supreme craftsmanship, Peter Shaw was able accurately to make a new chassis and front axle. Similarly, while he crafted bodies for the Sutherland and Birkin cars from the surviving bodywork panels, he also built a new two-seater body for this car. Using his contacts in the pre-war community and knowledge of the Maserati marque, he found numerous other detail features: such remarkable finds as an original aero screen, original oil tank, and the exquisitely designed water filler cap, all of which have ensured that the finished car was as true to form as it could be. Once completed, Shaw registered his car for the road and would campaign it for many years, proudly using it on the Mille Miglia in 1987. In 1999 he elected to sell it to the previous owner, Willem van Huystee. As with all of Mr van Huystee's cars, using the Maserati was his highest priority. Not satisfied with the car's performance as acquired, he sent it to legendary mechanical engineer Chris Leydon. Mr Leydon carried out a total rebuild of the engine while adhering to the owner's clear directive that all of its original components should be preserved and restored. This task proved to be a huge undertaking, but nevertheless the engine with its numbered crankcase was restored and returned to working order, as was the gearbox and rear axle, thus preserving the car's drive train. Following this work's completion, the Maserati was enthusiastically campaigned by Mr van Huystee, becoming a common sight at events ranging from road tours to concours, including the Pittsburgh Vintage Grand Prix at Lime Rock, Pocono; the Grand Ascent Hill Climb at Hershey; the Amelia Island Concours d'Elegance; Meadowbrook Hall Concours; and at Radnor Hunt. Over the years, its regular use has given the car an appealing patina, which seems appropriate for a historic Grand Prix car. It is currently kitted out with full road equipment, including cycle mudguards and headlamps. Throughout his ownership, Shaw researched the 3-Litre cars extensively, a particular anomaly being that Maserati's own records did not specifically reference a car number '3004'. At this point, based on current research, it seems likely that the crankcase '3004' was fitted to car '3001' by 1938 when the car began its spell in the UK, but its earlier history is unknown at this point in time. Its past owners believed that the origins of '3004' are one particular 8C that is visually documented in period but unaccounted for in history/number terms, this being a wide-chassis single-seater, identifiable by its body's higher tail. Importantly, that car still had mechanical brakes in its later guise, whereas the others were converted to hydraulics and their chassis drilled accordingly. in March 2016 the car was bought by the current vendor, the Maserati has been used only sparingly. The car starts and runs instantly and performed very well during the recent photo shoot where it was taken out on the road. It is currently registered in the Netherlands. Many of these important Maserati Grand Prix cars are now in long-term private or museum ownership, seldom seen or offered on the open market. Here we present a remarkable and rare opportunity to experience all the drama and excitement of owning and driving one of the earliest Maseratis, painstakingly restored by the finest marque expert with an exceptional eye for detail, and painstakingly maintained since. It is a car that can be raced, road-toured or simply taken out for the sheer thrill of it!

title: 1948 Bentley MkVI Special to 3/4½-Litre Tourer Specification Chassis no. B295CD Engine no. to be advised
description: 1948 Bentley MkVI Special to 3/4½-Litre Tourer Specification Registration no. XV 3230 Chassis no. B295CD Engine no. to be advised • Constructed over the last few years • New 10' 10" chassis by Peter Butler • New Gurney Nutting-style body • All major parts rebuilt With characteristic humility 'W O' was constantly amazed by the enthusiasm of later generations for the products of Bentley Motors Limited, and it is testimony to the soundness of his engineering design skills that so many of his products have survived. From the humblest of beginnings in a mews garage off Baker Street, London in 1919, the Bentley rapidly achieved fame as an exciting fast touring car, well able to compete with the best of European and American sports cars in the tough world of motor sport in the 1920s. Bentley's domination at Le Mans in 1924, 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 is legendary, and one can only admire the Herculean efforts of such giants as Woolf Barnato, Jack Dunfee, Tim Birkin and Sammy Davis, consistently wrestling the British Racing Green sports cars to victory. W O Bentley proudly unveiled the new 3-litre car bearing his name on Stand 126 at the 1919 Olympia Motor Exhibition, the prototype engine having fired up for the first time just a few weeks earlier. Bentley's four-cylinder 'fixed head' engine incorporated a single overhead camshaft, four-valves per cylinder and a bore/stroke of 80x149mm. Twin ML magnetos provided the ignition and power was transmitted via a four-speed gearbox with right-hand change. The pressed-steel chassis started off with a wheelbase of 9' 9½" then adopted dimensions of 10' 10" ('Standard Long') in 1923, the shorter frame being reserved for the TT Replica and subsequent Speed Model. Rear wheel brakes only were employed up to 1924 when four-wheel Perrot-type brakes were introduced. In only mildly developed form, this was the model that was to become a legend in motor racing history and which, with its leather-strapped bonnet, classical radiator design and British Racing Green livery, has become the archetypal Vintage sports car. Early success in the 1922 Isle of Man Tourist Trophy, when Bentleys finished 2nd, 4th, and 5th to take the Team Prize, led to the introduction of the TT Replica (later known as the Speed Model) on the existing 9' 9½" wheelbase, short standard chassis. However, by the middle of the decade the 3-Litre's competitiveness was on the wane and this, together with the fact that too many customers had been tempted to fit unsuitably heavy coachwork to the excellent 3-Litre chassis rather than accept the expense and complexity of Bentley's 6½-litre 'Silent Six', led to the introduction of the '4½'. The new 4½-Litre model effectively employed the chassis, transmission and brakes of the 3-Litre, combined with an engine that was in essence two-thirds of the six-cylinder 6½-litre unit. Thus the new four-cylinder motor retained the six's 100x140mm bore/stroke and Bentley's familiar four-valves-per-cylinder fixed-'head architecture, but reverted to the front-end vertical camshaft drive of the 3-Litre. Over the years many 3-Litre models have been updated with the '4½' engine. This particular car was constructed over the last few years by the vendor and incorporates a new 10' 10" wheelbase 3-litre style chassis by Peter Butler. The engine combines parts from both 3-litre and 4½-litre units, and drives via a C-type gearbox with added overdrive. Our vendor advises us that all major parts have been rebuilt: engine, water pump, radiator, both axles, steering, brakes, etc, etc. All components are described as 'Vintage renewed', with the exception of the connecting rods and engine bearings, which are new. The Gurney Nutting-style body is new also. The car is registered as a 1948 Bentley on the V5, and a chassis tag with the number B295CD is fitted to the car. Prospective buyers should make their own enquiries regards the registration of this particular lot.

title: 1931 Bentley 4½ Liter Supercharged Tourer Chassis no. MS 3928 Engine no. MS 3921
description: 1931 Bentley 4½ Liter Supercharged Tourer Replica coachwork in the Birkin Le Mans Style Chassis no. MS 3928 Engine no. MS 3921 "P" - Special formalities are required to bid on this lot. Contact Client Services at +1 (323) 850 7500 or bids.us@bonhams.com at least 48 hours in advance of the auction for registration and bidding options. 4½ Liter SOHC Inline 4-Cylinder Engine - 4 Overhead Valves Per Cylinder Factory Delivered High-compression Specification Amherst Villiers Roots Type IV Supercharger 182bhp with 10lbs Boost at 3,900rpm 4-Speed 'C' Type Gearbox Front and Rear Leaf Spring Suspension *One of the original 50 production 'Blower' Bentleys *Formerly in famous Charles R.J. Noble Collection for more than 47 years *Iconic Performance Bentley Model *Matching Numbers original crankcase included with the car *Presented in Desirable Birkin Le Mans Racing Guise THE SUPERCHARGED 4½ LITER BENTLEY The "Blower" Bentley is one of the most masculine, muscular, and sporting motorcars ever built. Where some companies hid their superchargers behind the radiator grill, the Bentley wears it right out front, and that statement alone says it all about the car and its creators. First shown at the 1929 London Motor Show, it was developed as a private venture by 'Bentley Boy' Sir Henry 'Tim' Birkin in order to extract more performance from the proven 4½-Liter model, which was becoming outclassed by its rivals on the racetracks of Europe. His aim was to produce a car that would enable British drivers to continue to win races as spectacularly as the 4½-Liter that had won the 1928 Le Mans 24-Hour race. The supercharger installation was engineered by the brilliant Amherst Villiers, who modestly claimed that it was 'recognized in engineering circles as a definite landmark in automobile construction.' W.O. Bentley never supported the development of the supercharged car and was quoted as saying how much he 'disliked the easy short cut provided by the supercharger,' preferring to increase engine capacity, as evidenced by the 6½-Liter and 8-Liter cars. He preferred reducing front-end weight by using Elektron castings. Fortunately 'W.O.' did not control the purse strings at Bentley Motors, and the influence of Birkin, backed by the fabulously wealthy Honorable Dorothy Paget and Woolf Barnato, saw the Supercharged 4½-Litre Bentley come to fruition. Its potential was emphatically demonstrated when Tim Birkin took 2nd place in the French Grand Prix at Pau with his supercharged 4½-Liter tourer amid a field of monoposto GP racers. The production Blower Bentley was intrinsically linked to Le Mans, quite simply Bentley Motors built the 50 production supercharged 4½-Liter Bentleys to support the homologation of five Birkin team cars. When Birkin campaigned his Blower at Le Mans in 1930 his car retired after 138 laps and almost 20 hours of Racing. But, in an incredibly Heroic effort he passed the leading 7-Liter Supercharged Mercedes driven by Rudolf Caracciola on the Hunaudières Straight. The pass at 125mph shocked Caracciola and caused him to overstress the Mercedes engine in efforts to keep up with the Bentleys. This effort and the continual Bentley pressure caused the Mercedes to fail and withdraw from the race with a blown gasket Birkin therefore eased the way for the Works Speed Six to win the marque's final Le Mans victory until this century. It should be noted that Birkin set the Fastest Lap in the Race and broke the Lap Record at 89.696mph in his No. 9 supercharged 4½ liter Bentley. His time of 6 min. 48 sec. was never beaten on the 10.153 mile circuit. The fifty production cars were fitted with an Amherst Villiers Supercharger Mark IV, of Roots type with twin paddle rotors, which drew mixture from twin SU carburetors and was driven off the front of the crankshaft, the latter having been substantially strengthened to accommodate the increased power. With 9½ lbs boost at 3,500rpm the blown Bentley developed 175bhp, a healthy increase over the production 4½-Liter's 110 horsepower, while with 10lbs boost at 3,900rpm, 182bhp was produced. Despite representing the epitome of 'Boys Own' motoring and providing the heart and soul of the hobby, selling the requisite fifty cars that had needed to be built in the dire economic climate of the late 1920s proved hard work for Bentley Motors. As a result of this, though it may seem improbable today, not all were sporting tourers in period. Among the few cars that were capable of 100mph on the open road. Blowers have always been regarded as the Supercars of their era. In period the British magazine Motor Sport spoke of the Blower's 'remarkable acceleration' and 'ancestry of well-tried racers' calling it 'a car for the connoisseur of sporting cars...' - Nothing has changed today! THE CAR OFFERED This fabulous Blower embodies every ounce of the Bentley, Birkin and Le Mans spirit following an exacting rebuild with a great eye for the details on the racing Bentleys of the Cricklewood age. The ledgers of the Cricklewood works survive to this day, with the result that tracing the origins of these cars is a relatively straightforward exercise. On file for SM 3928 is a copy of its original build sheet which confirms that it was delivered new as a handsome Gurney Nutting Drophead Coupe built to Weymann (lightweight) principles. Images of the car as new show that it was a truly understated car and undeniably a 'Wolf in Sheep's Clothing', which must have grabbed some 'double takes' when it hared around in 1931, not least as its supercharger was discretely hidden under a valance. Agent Jack Olding & Co. Ltd handled its original sale, selling it to W.C. Gordon Black of Fife, Scotland in the spring of 1931. On the technical side its record notes its original engine to have been number SM 3921, Supercharger number 128 and it to have had a D-Box as new. According to the Vintage Bentley expert Clare Hay, ownerships after Gordon Black followed in 1934, the car being sold through Rowland Smith in this period albeit the owner is not known; J.L. Fawdon purchased the Blower in 1948 owning it for 2 years before it passed to a T.P. Balch. Squadron Leader William Kent was its owner from 1952 to 1954, an experience which he recounted to Bentley historian Clare Hay in a letter in 1993 he 'thought it magnificent' despite lacking 'creature comforts, and 10-11mpg'. 'It had such unusual and I thought ideal coachwork' 'and the body panels, except for the bonnet and boot, faced in black patent leather and soft to the touch' (confirming its Weymann design). He must have toured on the European continent as he praised its large headlights and dipping system 'for the Grand Touring on French Roads.' Its next owner was D.C. Wilson, who owned it for a short time in 1954 before passing it on to A.J. Sterling Wakeley of London who kept the car through to March 1st, 1961. It was owned briefly by R.J. Whittaker, the former owner Charles R.J. Noble acquiring it from him on Halloween 1961 as a rolling chassis. Later that decade a restoration was begun to put it into the famous 'Birkin Blower' guise, the lightweight fabric skinned bodywork being completed by Restor Ltd. and the various mechanical aspects being attended to by respected restorers of the day such as Hoffman & Burton and Jeff Huckle. By this point it had lost its gearbox, and a C-Type unit was fitted being number 6926 which had begun life in the fourth from last Speed Six (HM2867) and was therefore up to the job. Its restoration was completed in the middle of the 1980s and the car was shown in this freshly finished form in 1987 at the Bentley Driver's Club Kensington Meet in Kensington Gardens. Shortly after this the car was brought to its American ownership, remaining in this country ever since. In the mid-2000s, a full mechanical refurbishment of the engine was carried out in this country by noted British engineer Tony Wardle, who flew to the USA to undertake the work. During which the decision was made to replace its crankcase using a replacement casting supplied by John Bentley, with new insert bearings as opposed to white metal and a new block. At this point the original numbered crankcase was separated from the car. Although away from the car for a number of years this key component has now been repatriated to the car ensuring its matching numbers, chassis/engine status, which is shared also with front, back axle banjo (not turret) and steering box all stamped MS 3928. After 47 years of Noble ownership, where at one point it shared stable with 3 other Blowers for a tally of 10% of the surviving examples, MS 3928 was sold publicly in 2008, joining a prominent collection of competition and sports cars. In this custody, the Bentley has been exercised and kept ready for use, albeit its actual use has been relatively modest. Today the car emerges for sale, having been off the radar and in a mere two ownerships in 62 years. Its rebuild of the 1980s is now well-settled, adding some patina and general character to the car. On a recent test drive the Blower was shown to start promptly on multiple occasions and continues to be an enjoyable and strong performer. Beyond their 'Boys Own' looks, Vintage Bentleys are incredibly usable machines, they have the physical road presence to carry their own today on any road, be it single lane or freeway, and ample performance to hold their own in the performance stakes too. Accordingly, there are numerous events for which they can be used from those of the North American Vintage Bentley Club, to even long distance tours such as the Colorado Grand. They are also supported by an international roster of engineers who can supply key spares to keep them on the road. With the recent Centenary of Le Mans, images of the iconic endurance racers that campaigned over those 100 years were recalled. Of course, the Vintage Bentley epitomizes the late 1920s era, and of all those that you might want to be behind the wheel of, it is a Blower such as this that is the most coveted, their racing intentions dictated their production run and they are intrinsically linked to Le Mans.

title: 1933 Bentley 3½ Liter Sports Tourer Coachwork by Vanden Plas Chassis no. B1AE Engine no. 2ZBA
description: The First Production Derby Bentley, Company Trials Car 1933 Bentley 3½ Liter Sports Tourer Coachwork by Vanden Plas Chassis no. B1AE Engine no. 2ZBA 3,669cc Inline 6-Cylinder Engine Twin SU carburetors, approximately 115bhp at 3,800rpm 4-Speed Manual Transmission Front and Rear Leaf Spring Suspension 4-Wheel Servo Assisted Drum Brakes *One of the most important Bentleys in the history of the marque *The unique pivotal link between WO and Derby Eras of Bentley *Extensively documented *Feature car for company brochure, Motor Sport and other magazines *Never restored, retains original interior and many original finishes *Not displayed or toured since 1996 THE MOTORCAR OFFERED Bonhams proudly presents this unique Bentley motorcar and in doing so provides an opportunity to collectors which has not been offered to the market since it was acquired by the current owner's grandfather in 1962. Upon purchasing B1AE the buyer would be only the fifth owner since the car's manufacture. It is a potentially generational chance to purchase a car of immense importance to the history of the Bentley brand, the first production Bentley, chassis number B1AE – the original 'Silent Sports Car'. The first car, No. 1, in the first production series, AE, of the entirely new Bentley Motors (1931) Ltd., it was one of three cars used predominantly by the company to promote the new era of Bentley to the world and the only one that would wear open touring coachwork. That carefully penned design was a modern 1930s take on the vintage look by none other than Vanden Plas, who had provided bodies through the 1920s for W.O. Bentley. In this and so many respects, it is the critical link between the two main eras of their production. That transition had begun in 1931, when the receivers were brought into Bentley, following Woolf Barnato's withdrawal of funding. It had been a sad fall for grace from the once invincible Bentley Boys, who in 1930 had claimed their fourth win at Le Mans in the legendary 'hare and tortoise' race, where Sir Henry 'Tim' Birkin had charged away goading the Mercedes SSKs into burning out their superchargers and allowing the Works Speed Sixes to come home victorious. The worldwide depression, the fall in sales leading to Woolf Barnato finally pulling his funding nearly led to the destruction of one of the greatest names in British motorsport. As luck would have it, former competitor Rolls-Royce outbid others including Napier to ensure the perpetuation of Bentley. From 1931 through to the spring of 1933, the Rolls engineers worked tirelessly to refine a new Bentley motorcar, and when they launched, it was received to universal acclaim, even 'WO', who was part of the team that tested the new car extensively is quoted as saying - "Taking all things into consideration, I would rather own this Bentley car than any car produced under that name" Bentley chose a careful path of marketing for they were keen that the new model maintained the same appeal for sportsmen, and to that end the car was newly built from the ground up, despite perception the engine having little in common with the contemporary Rolls-Royce. It was about true road performance, power, handling, good brakes and above all refinement and quietness of running. To ensure that the 'dots were joined' from the Vintage Bentley to the new cars, they made cars available to those who were associated with the predecessors. The car that they used for much of this promotion was 'B1AE', which was registered by the company with the distinctive license plate 'ALU 321', the prefix perhaps referencing its lightweight aluminum coachwork, which for added draw was finished in silver paintwork. By nature, its open sports body both showed the Bentley to be a sportsman's car, but it also allowed the luminaries of the day that they invited to test it to be visible for photographs while they did so. Proud of the model, Bentley Motors put out an extensive brochure entitled 'Some Opinions', and there in print, the likes of Earl Howe, Malcolm Campbell and others can be seen exercising this very car. But, perhaps the most surprising face behind the wheel is none other than Woolf Barnato, who like the others is all smiles as he pilots B1AE. Some of the pertinent quotes in the publication are: "Words cannot convey the charm or suave speed in this new car, its docility when docility is desired, its devouring bite into the speedometer reading when that is demanded, and its wonderous response to braking when checked from 90 mph" - Universe "After the conclusion of my run I came away full of enthusiasm, as the new 3 ½ litre Bentley is the most amazing proposition which it has ever fallen to my lot to handle. Although in the past I have owned several Bentley cars, all of which have afforded utmost satisfaction, never has such a Bentley been turned out previously to compare with the new product" – Sir Malcolm Campbell in The Field "Here is an entirely new conception of a sports car. The 3 ½ litre Bentley gives a hitherto undreamt-of combination of performance and comfort." – The Sketch Earl Howe's test was far longer, B1AE being loaned to him for a complete weekend. His commentary to the then company director Lord Herbert Scott extends over six carefully detailed pages of words, copies of which are in the large file of material that has accrued over its lifetime. He opens: "I really don't know how to thank you and Mr. Cowan for your very great kindness in giving me one of the most wonderful treats that I have had for a very long time, namely the use of one of the new Bentleys for two whole days." The Bentley is featured in numerous other publications, it was the subject car for Motorsport magazine's 1933 test of the model, where it is pictured over the caption 'A Masterpiece of Sports Car Construction', again, they too wax lyrical of its merits. "To get into a motorcar one has never driven before, to take it up to its maximum revs. in all its gears and to brake and swing round corners with the utmost joie de vivre, one has either to be lacking in imagination or very confident in the car's controllability. The second needless to say was the reason when we first took the wheel of the new Bentley." "From the start we felt perfectly at home in the car, and the "rightness" of direction and handling were such as one only expects in a car tuned for racing." They continue to talk of a secondary test on a wet day, with poor visibility – "After a gentle beginning... we discovered that under all circumstances the front wheels kept to the intended path, and the tail showed no tendency to slide. Encouraged by this, speed was increased to 80-85 mph without any feeling of insecurity, and fast bends at 75mph seemed quite safe. These speeds were quickly reached using the excellent gearbox with its quick changes and its silent running ratios." "The car was as comfortable on Brooklands as on the road, and the speedometer, which was accurate, showed 93mph on most parts of the track." "By reason of its low build, the Bentley looks remarkably neat and handy. Actually it is only 4 inches shorter than the old 4 ½ litre, but the passengers sit closer together." "This ... seems to be reflected in the way the car handles, for one can dodge in and out of traffic or swoop round right angle bends in a way usually associated with an 8ft 6 wheelbase." "The open Vanden Plas body which was fitted to the car we tested was a handsome and practical production in keeping with the high quality of the chassis. The long and well-louvred bonnet and scuttle, two door body cut away for the front passengers, and straight-line quarters and hoods are sporting in line, and the long sweeping wings afford excellent protection. The rear panel, which carried the spare wheel, is hinged at the bottom. When opened it discloses a luggage space large enough for several suitcases. The hood side-screens are carried in a pocket on the inside of the hinged panel." Culminating in the comments of – "No effort has been spared to perfect the 3½ litre Bentley, and it is indeed the car for the connoisseur of fast travel. From every point of view the new car meets the modern need for a fast, lively and smoothly running sports car of the highest quality, and the interest with which its coming was awaited has been equalled by the enthusiasm of its reception by those who have tried it." But, the best testamentary of all comes from the Brooklands periodical Air and Travel where under an illustration of 'ALU 321' racing along a country road they state – "Imagine the best sports car you have ever driven, add something to its performance, and let every aspect of its running be carried out in complete silence and with Rolls-Royce smoothness, and that is as near as you will get to an appreciation of the 3½ litre Bentley without having tried one." Bentley Motors kept the first production Bentley for nearly 2 years, before the model was due for its own revisions, and taste in coachwork had evolved to be altogether less sporting, leading to their introduction of its successor, the 4¼ Liter in March 1936. When they sold B1AE, it was purchased by one Gordon Thomas of Taunton and later Wolverhampton. Mr. Thomas recounts in later correspondence that he found the silver paintwork to be all too garish for his tastes and he had the car painted in the black that it still wears to this day. For more than 17 years he remained its custodian before selling the car to the author Eric Williams. Mr. Williams is best known for his book The Wooden Horse , but if one dives into another of his works novels, Complete and Free, which is loosely autobiographical, one immediately finds reference to the Bentley in the opening phrase – "The old open car sat low on her springs under the weight of luggage...', a few pages later, it refers to Williams taking the car back to the Works previously before he began his trip - 'Majestic white-haired Mr. Clarke (Nobby), proud veteran of the old Bentley racing days' had had the car checked over for him. "Have you had it in before" Williams had asked, 'Course we have. B1AE. She's the first we made. I could ... tell you every repair that's been done on her. And that's not much' In 1959 Mr. Williams decided to go on a world tour, which he knew would be extended and would leave the Bentley unattended to for a couple of years, in anticipation of this he elected to put B1AE up for sale. Amazing though it may seem today, there were no takers, which interestingly led to a column in The Field pontificating – "Is there no one in Britain rich enough, romantic enough and robust enough to buy the first Rolls-Bentley. Must this superb open tourer go to America?" As it happened, it was acquired then by Guy Lawrence, a successful car trader who lived at Little Easton Manor in the town of Dunmow, who re-registered the car in that County, Essex, with the license number RB 1933. After approximately 3 years, he elected to sell the car. The Bentley arrived in Charles Follett's esteemed Mayfair showroom in 1962, and it was there that the current owner's grandfather caught sight of her. Appreciating both her beauty and understanding her importance, the car was quickly purchased in September 1962, and indeed it did migrate to this country. Over the course of the next sixty years, the Bentley has been cared for by its current owner's family, initially the car was toured on occasions, and even participated in key events, such as The Derby Bentley Diamond Jubilee in the UK in 1993. A few years after that on the death of his father, the Bentley was put into climate-controlled storage and has seen care rather than use for the ensuing 30 years. As acquired, the Bentley had survived its first 3 decades in remarkably good order, its newer paintwork was wearing well, and its original upholstery had never been changed and was still there in its azure blue scheme, which had originally provided contrast to the svelte silver paint. Fortunately for us today, it has remained that way ever since. When appropriate, or necessary, very minor repair was made to its interior, but it still retains an entirely authentic feel and even the original side screens, piped in that same color are present. Viewed closely, it seems that the original silvery finish remains under the black paintwork in places, particularly on the bonnet/hood. After its period of slumber, the Bentley has recently been checked over and made to silently roar on the roads once again. On the road, even after 25 years of slumber, the Bentley has an extraordinary aura. The motto of The Silent Sports Car is immediately apparent, as there is very little road noise, and the car has literally no rattles or scuttle shake, it just purrs down the road absorbing bumps nonchalantly. All the while, the Bentley is incredibly lively, with plenty of power on tap and its gearbox is silky smooth, the brakes are precise and work quickly. Behind the wheel, the period commentaries and road reports echo in your head and how magical it is to enjoy those visceral experiences first-hand nearly 90 years later. Perhaps because it has never been restored, perhaps as the factory car it was tweaked a bit more than standard, but whatever the recipe, the combination makes for an absolutely brilliant and rewarding drive which is highly recommended. In every respect this is an incredible car, from its highly desirable early sports touring Vanden Plas coachwork to its simple provenance and its intrinsic originality and condition, it would surely be thought of as one of the finest of the model, even before one considers its importance as the pivotal link between the WO and Derby eras. A car in a category of its own, extensively documented from day one, and unseen for a quarter of a century, it would certainly be welcomed around the world at any major event and could easily stand as a focal point in any major collection. After all, who wouldn't want to own and experience a car which WO Bentley himself would rather have owned than any prior that had carried his name.

title: 1929 Bentley 4½ LITER TO SUPERCHARGED SPECIFICATIONS REPLICA LE MANS STYLE COACHWORK Chassis no. AB 3669 Engine no. (See catalog)
description: 1929 Bentley 4½ LITER TO SUPERCHARGED SPECIFICATIONS REPLICA LE MANS STYLE COACHWORK Chassis no. AB 3669 Engine no. (See catalog) 5,200cc SOHC 12 Valve Inline 4-Cylinder Engine Amherst Villers Type Roots Supercharger Approx. 200bhp with 10lbs Boost at 3,900rpm 4-Speed 'D' Type Close-ratio Gearbox (see catalog) Front and Rear Leaf Spring Suspension with Andre Hartford Shocks 4-Wheel Drum Brakes *Original 4½ liter Bentley upgraded to 'Works' 'Blower' Spec *Superbly prepared over the course of a decade *Executed by a noted engineer and Bentley expert *Proven performer in vintage racing and rallying *As fast as a vintage Bentley gets THE BENTLEY 4½ LITER SUPERCHARGED The "Blower" Bentley is one of the most masculine, muscular and sporting motorcars ever built. Where some companies hid their superchargers behind the radiator grill, the Bentley wears it right out front, and that statement alone says it all about the car and its creators. First shown at the 1929 London Motor Show, it was developed as a private venture by 'Bentley Boy' Sir Henry 'Tim' Birkin in order to extract more performance from the proven 4½-Liter model, which was becoming outclassed by its rivals on the racetracks of Europe. His aim was to produce a British car that would enable British drivers to continue to win races as spectacularly as the 4½-Liter that had won the 1928 Le Mans 24-Hour race. The supercharger installation was engineered by the brilliant Amherst Villiers, who modestly claimed that it was 'recognized in engineering circles as a definite landmark in automobile construction.' W.O. Bentley never supported the development of the supercharged car and was quoted as saying how much he 'disliked the easy short cut provided by the supercharger,' preferring to increase engine capacity, as evidenced by the 6½-Liter and 8-Liter cars. He preferred reducing front-end weight by using Elektron castings. Fortunately, 'W.O.' did not control the purse strings at Bentley Motors, and the influence of Birkin, backed by the fabulously wealthy Honorable Dorothy Paget and Woolf Barnato, saw the Supercharged 4½-Litre Bentley come to fruition. The fifty production cars were fitted with an Amherst Villiers Supercharger Mark IV, of Roots type with twin paddle rotors, which drew mixture from twin SU carburetors and was driven off the front of the crankshaft, the latter having been substantially strengthened to accommodate the increased power. With 9½ lbs boost at 3,500rpm the blown Bentley developed 175bhp, a healthy increase over the production 4½-Liter's 110 horsepower, while with 10lbs boost at 3,900rpm, 182bhp was produced. Despite representing the epitome of 'Boys Own' motoring and providing the heart and soul of the hobby, selling the requisite fifty cars that had needed to be built in the dire economic climate of the late 1920s proved hard work for Bentley Motors. As a result of this, though it may seem improbable today, not all were sporting tourers. Some 17 were delivered as drophead coupes and even closed Saloon cars. Among the few cars that were capable of 100mph on the open road. Blowers have always been regarded as the Supercars of their era. In period the British magazine Motor Sport spoke of the Blower's 'remarkable acceleration' and 'ancestry of well-tried racers' calling it 'a car for the connoisseur of sporting cars...' - Nothing has changed today! THE MOTORCAR OFFERED Presented here is a machine that was painstakingly engineered to be the finest performing Vintage Bentley. This project was executed over the course of a decade by a well-known American engineer and Bentley expert in conjunction with Neil Davies Racing in the UK. Chassis AB3699 was delivered in January of 1929 to WL Van Allen. As new, it was fitted with fabric saloon coachwork by Weymann and wore registration YE 312. Vintage Bentley enthusiast Charlie Lowe Jr. acquired AB3699 in the 1950s, and it was from him that the present owner acquired the car in the early 2000s. Starting with this proper, original 4½ liter, the arduous process of locating as many correct Blower specification items began. To have the proper "Works" specification, an original Speed-Six rear axle was located, along with an original works style hood. A new Neil Davies Racing 5.2 liter heavy sump engine was commissioned. Large "Works'' specification aluminum SU carburetors feed the early John Bentley Engineering supercharger which produces 8-10psi of induction pressure. The engine's output is estimated to be in excess of 200bhp. The motor is mated to a fresh D series gearbox, and the original matching numbered C 'box is included with the car. A proper Le Mans VDP style tourer body was constructed in the US and finished and trimmed in the UK. The coachwork was mated with large Works-type fuel tank, cycle fenders, original Zeiss headlamps and an original, numbered works type hood. The purposeful dashboard is resplendent with the full complement of large Works-style instruments and original Air Ministry switchgear. The chassis is perhaps the one area the Bentley shows the most engineering input and refinement. The tracking is razor sharp, and the suspension is perfectly tuned for neutral handling and phenomenal grip. The leaf springs are all 'Blower' specification heavy units, with 'Blower' specific shocks. The frame is reinforced with Works 'Le Mans' style truss work. The light steering is the most surprising aspect of this car -an untypical characteristic of a Blower, but this is not any ordinary Blower. This level of refinement is a testament to the painstaking attention that went into sorting out the front-end. To stop this potent machine, a full set of late pattern Bentley self-energizing brakes and Alfin drums are fitted on all four-wheels. A recent outing on the Thompson Motor Speedway road course showed the phenomenal performance this Bentley possesses. A Bonhams specialist well versed in vintage Bentleys found it to be as quick as any Bentley he had ever driven with incredible grip and light steering. In experienced hands the car devoured the track with truly impressive speed and handling. Since completion it has been a regular participant at the Lime Rock Vintage Festival race meetings and has also taken part in the California Mille. This is a superbly prepared car, reported to be absolutely on the button by its seller and is ready to enjoy. A real 4½ Liter Bentley uprated to the ultimate Blower specification, this impeccably prepared machine is not to be missed.

title: A Group of Grace Kelly Photographs
description: A Group of Grace Kelly Photographs Comprising 6 gelatin silver photographs, all but one being vintage 1950s, 2 with original snipes/captions on verso, including 2 of Kelly in a white negligee, one of her as a child with her siblings (printed later), one of her hiking in Palm Springs, one of her holding her Academy Award for The Country Girl (1954), and one closeup. Together with an 8 x 10 in. color transparency closeup of Kelly and a vintage duplicate of the black-and-white closeup photo. Grace Kelly was at the peak of her celebrity in 1956 when she left her show business career to marry Prince Rainier of Monaco in one of the biggest news stories of the decade. Though she toyed with returning to making films during the years she was Princess of Monaco, the people of Monaco strongly opposed this suggestion. High Society , released in 1956, was her last film. 8 x 10 in. each

title: Howard Kelly's copy with his bookplate. Kerckring, Theodor (1640-93). Spicilegium anatomicum, continens observationum anatomicarum rariorum centuriam unam, nec non osteogeniam foetuum... Amsterdam: Sumptibus Andreae Frisii, 1670.
description: Jeremy Norman, History of Science and Technology. Howard Kelly's copy with his bookplate. Kerckring, Theodor (1640-93). Spicilegium anatomicum, continens observationum anatomicarum rariorum centuriam unam, nec non osteogeniam foetuum... Amsterdam: Sumptibus Andreae Frisii, 1670. 4to (237 x 188 mm). Engraved frontispiece and 9 engraved plates; engraved text illustrations. Vellum ca. 1670, lower edge of spine chipped, inner front hinge cracked, some spotting and soiling. Front margin of frontispiece repaired, light foxing and toning, a few edges frayed but very good. Provenance: Howard A. Kelly (1858-1943) (bookplate); Terence Cavanagh, onetime librarian at the Duke University Hospital Library (bookplate). First Edition. "Kerckring made important investigations on the development of the foetal bones. He was the first to describe the large ossicle sometimes present at the lambdoidal suture; his name is remembered in the valvulae conniventes of the small intestine, previously described by Fallopius" (Garrison-Morton.com 383). The book's chapter on osteogenia foetum "presumes to give an account of the fetal skeleton from the second month to the end of gestation. [Kerckring] stated correctly that only a little of the skeleton can be found during the second month, and rightly concluded that the bones arise from a transformation of membranous into cartilaginous parts and of these into bone" (Meyer, The Rise of Embryology, p. 297). This copy is from the library of Howard A. Kelly, one of the original "Four Physicians" of Johns Hopkins, who was a major figure in the development of abdominal and gynecological surgery.

title: Seven Passages to a Flight, an Artists Book with a Story Quilt by Faith Ringgold, the Publisher's Own Copy. RINGGOLD, FAITH. 1930-2024. Seven Passages to a Flight. San Diego, CA: Brighton Press, 1995.
description: Printed & Manuscript Americana Seven Passages to a Flight , an Artists Book with a Story Quilt by Faith Ringgold, the Publisher's Own Copy. RINGGOLD, FAITH. 1930-2024. Seven Passages to a Flight. San Diego, CA: Brighton Press, 1995. Square folio (233 x 191 mm). 9 hand-painted etchings with multicolored pochoir borders and text, printed on linen. Original cloth binding by David Brock; original painted clamshell box with fabric inlays. Provenance: Bill Kelly, co-founder and director of Brighton Press. Provenance : Bill Kelly, co-founder and director of Brighton Press. ONE OF 15 COPIES WITH A HAND-SEWN QUILT PAINTED AND STENCILED BY HAND, THE PUBLISHER'S OWN COPY . Limited edition, number 3 of 30 copies SIGNED BY FAITH RINGGOLD . THE QUILT SIGNED AND DATED BY FAITH RINGGOLD : "Faith Ringgold 9/15/98," (overall 1260 x 1065 mm). The 9 hand-painted and -stenciled etchings in the artists book, reproduced on the quilt, were created by Faith Ringgold, Michele Burgess, Bill Kelly, and Nelle Martin. The imagery on the quilt is flanked at top and bottom with Ringgold's text, all of which is quilted in a diamond pattern that mimics the geometric border. This is all surrounded by a patchwork border with two layers of piping. From the printed limitation statement on the quilt: "This autobiographical quilt is comprised of the nine etchings and text from Seven Passages to a Flight , an artist's book by Faith Ringgold. The etchings were printed on linen and stenciled by hand. The text was set in Perpetua and printed letterpress. Both the book and the quilt were published and produced by Brighton Press, San Diego, California in 1995-1996. There is a limited edition of thirty quilts, ten numbered in Roman numerals and twenty lettered A-T." According to the Brighton Press records, however, although thirty quilts were planned, only 15 were produced. Other examples of the quilt are held by Museum of Modern Art, The San Diego Museum of Art, and the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art at Cornell. The text and illustrations in Seven Passages to a Flight are printed on linen, a nod to Ringgold's celebrated narrative quilts. Ringgold's use of fabrics with painting was an intentional move away traditional European modes of storytelling. Indeed, her first experience of 14th- and 15th-century Tibetan thangkas, during a visit to the Rijksmuseum in 1972, inspired her to include fabric borders around her own work. She learned how to quilt in the Black tradition from her mother, clothing designer Willie Posey Jones, and her grandmother, who had in turn learned it from her mother, Susie Shannon, an enslaved person. Seven Passages to a Flight is an autobiographical work that weaves the themes of race, gender, family, and the right to dream among the broader African American experience. Ringgold recalls her recurrent bouts of asthma as a child: "While I was recuperating in bed, my mother would give me crayons and paints to make pictures, and pieces of cloth to make sewn things. I loved to copy the beautiful engravings of presidents from my brother and sister's history books." As her artistic practice develops, she writes, "probably the first time I rewrote history in my art was when I painted a mural of some black and white boys sitting together eating watermelon with George Washington's soldiers at Valley Forge." According to critic and curator Darla Migan, "Through her imaginative investigations into narratives of heritage, stretching back and forth across the Atlantic in different media, Faith Ringgold's artwork -- paintings, drawings, masks, books, and her latest inventions... -- questions America's historical formations, commemorates the tragic loss of life in the fight for equality, and celebrates the ongoing struggle for civil rights wherever that struggle is happening today. ...Rather than waiting for American history to canonize their significance or waiting for her own biography to surface, Ringgold moves against and within the legacy of the gallery exhibition to represent her personal journey as an artist " (D. Migan, "Looking but not seeing?," Texte Zur Kunst, September 2018, p.170, 173). WITH A SMALL PRINTER'S ARCHIVE , assembled by co-founder and director of Brighton Press, Bill Kelly, himself a painter, printmaker, and sculptor. The archive includes six proofs of the hand-colored etchings printed on five sheets of linen (one double-sided): two black-and-white proofs in an early state, two colored proofs printed without a border (one with pencil border outlines for the border), and two double-page spreads of text and etching printed within multicolored pochoir borders. Also included is the printer's mock-up of the binding boards, and a single sheet with a quote in Ringgold's hand inscribed five times ("My father said we tore up the pattern for that one F.R.").
