title: TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT. MUSSEY, REUBEN DIMOND. 1780-1866. Autograph Letter Signed, to Dr. Beverly R. Wellford, 3 pp, New York, August 18, 1853.
description: TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT. MUSSEY, REUBEN DIMOND. 1780-1866. Autograph Letter Signed, to Dr. Beverly R. Wellford, 3 pp, New York, August 18, 1853. Mussey writes, in part, " The enclosed paper will announce its object. The suggestion was made by a highly intelligent & influential member of our Association in this State, Dr. Blatchford of Troy, that if the ex-President ? the one now in office, should give their name to one guest such as the sheet contains, it might have influence with the Committee of Arrangements at St. Louis. It was thought it might even do more than a large list of other names that might with a little effort be procured. I have been to Astoria, the residence of Dr. [Alexander H.] Stevens, 6 miles from the city, but as he is to be absent a week or two, I send the paper to yourself, hoping that you might think so favorably as to append your name. Physicians, perhaps, more than any other class of men, have the opportunity of witnessing the effects of strong drink upon health, life & morals, & it should seem, that as they claim, & justly, belong to a philanthropic profession, they would always be ready to discourage, by every means in their power, the use of it as a beverage. I have no doubt that Dr. Stevens will place his name at the head of the list when handed the paper. I take this opportunity to thank you most cordially for your most excellent draft at our last meeting. It cannot fail to do great good, especially as it is to be published in our Transactions.... Very sincerely, Your friend, R. D. Mussey. " WITH: CROSBY, ALPHEUS B. An Address Commemorative of Reuben Dimond Mussey, M.D., LL.D. Manchester, New Hampshire: 1869. Pamphlet. Lacking wrappers. First edition. Browning, a few slight edge chips, old adhesive residue on verso of signature page (blank). Reuben Dimond Mussey received his M.D. from Dartmouth in 1805 and was a leading peripatetic medical teacher and practitioner throughout the first half of the nineteenth century. His biographer Alpheus Crosby explained, "It was as a surgeon that Dr. Mussey came to be most extensively known.... Both as an operative and scientific surgeon he attained a national reputation." Mussey was the fourth president of the American Medical Association (1850). "He was a total abstainer from the use of both tobacco and alcohol, and seems to have written more upon this subject than any other" (DAB 7(1):372-373.) Beverly Randolph Wellford (1797-1870) was an 1817 medical graduate of the University of Maryland. He was president of the American Medical Association in 1852, two years after Mussey served in that capacity. Kelly Burrage 895-896.

title: MUTTER, THOMAS DENT 1811-1859. Archive of items:
description: MUTTER, THOMAS DENT 1811-1859. Archive of items: 1. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, August 12, 1844. Mutter writes, " As I mainly wish a relic or two of Sir A. Cooper, and shall obtain them among the specimens already selected at the college, I do not think I will take the testis we looked at together ." 2. Manuscript notes in an interleaved book: Syllabus of the Course of Lectures on the Principles and Practice of Surgery, Delivered in the Jefferson Medical College, Philadelphia. Philadelphia: 1851. Half calf and boards. Front board detached, backstrip loose. Interleaved copy with copious notes by J. S. Weiser, who inscribed this copy in pencil (light) on the front free endpaper: " J. S. Weiser, Jefferson Medical College, 1853 ." 8vo. Half calf and marbled boards. Top cover detached. Chipping. 3. Manuscript notes in an interleaved book: Syllabus of the Course of Lectures on the Principles and Practice of Surgery, Delivered in the Jefferson Medical College, Philadelphia. Part I. Philadelphia: 1843. Half calf and boards. Interleaved copy with copious notes by Jacob l. Ziegler. 8vo. Half calf and marbled boards. Joints tender. 4. LEWIS, R.J. "Memoir of Thomas D. Mutter, M.D." 1859, 6pp. Extract from Medical and Surgical Reporter. 5. LINDGREN, LAURA, Editor. Mutter Museum: Historic Medical Photographs. New York: 2007. First edition, first printing. Thomas Dent Mutter "was probably the first in America to perform plastic operations to correct deformities" (Garrison-Morton-Norman 5743.2). He received his M.D. from the University of Pennsylvania in 1831, where he became professor of surgery. His huge personal collection of anatomical, pathological, and surgical specimens was acquired by the College of Physicians of Philadelphia and has become internationally known as the Mutter Museum. Pioneering English microscopist John Thomas Quekett (1815-1861) was assistant conservator of the Hunterian Museum of the Royal College of Surgeons. Astley Cooper (1768-1841) was the preeminent British surgeon of his generation. Among his many publications was a book on the testis (1830). Kelly Burrage 896-897. Josiah S. Weiser (1832-1863) lived in Oley, Berks County, Pennsylvania, when he was a student at Jefferson. Subsequently, he practiced in Shakopee, Minnesota. When he was twenty-nine years old, Weiser "was commissioned Chief Surgeon of the First Minnesota Mounted Rangers, on October 1, 1862. Dr. Weiser had been personally acquainted with many Sioux Indians in Minnesota, and when the Indians of Minnesota and the Dakotas rose against the Government in 1862, he felt he could be of use as a negotiator between them. General Sibley was ordered to North Dakota to put down the uprising and Dr. Weiser accompanied him as chief surgeon. 'When they came in contact with the enemy, previous to the Battle of Big Mound, an effort was made to bring about an understanding, and an amicable establishment of the difficulties. A parley was being held some 300 yards from the camp by representatives from both sides. Dr. Weiser was one of the party and while engaged in negotiating for peace was shot by an Indian and met almost immediate death" (Francis Packard, History of Medicine in the United States , 2nd editiom, Philadelphia 1931, 2:935-936). Weiser's death in July, 1863 caused negotiations to end and led to the Battle of Big Mound. See also Keenen, The Terrible Indian Wars of the West , 1998: 270-271. Weiser's book was subsequently owned by Dr. Kee Wakefield of Hutchinson, Minnesota and by the Library of the Ramsay County Medical Society. Jacob L. Ziegler (1822-1906) inscribed this copy in ink on the front free endpaper: "J. L. Ziegler, Jefferson Medical College, Phila. November 17, 1843." He graduated in 1844 and practiced medicine in Mt. Joy, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania for sixty-three years.

title: MICROSCOPY ARCHIVE. QUEKETT, JOHN THOMAS. 1815-1861. Extensive archive of letters to John Thomas Quekett and his brother Edwin John Quekett.
description: MICROSCOPY ARCHIVE. QUEKETT, JOHN THOMAS. 1815-1861. Extensive archive of letters to John Thomas Quekett and his brother Edwin John Quekett. 1.Bennett, John Hughes. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, Edinburgh, July 20, 1848. Bennett informs Quekett, "Last Thursday I was unanimously elected to the Chair of the Institutes of Medicine in this University and have now to return to you my warmest thanks for your kind testimonial on my behalf." Marginal tear with no loss. John Hughes Bennett (1812-1875) was one of Scotland's leading physicians, teachers, and authors. He published the first description of acute leukemia in 1845 and was elected chair of the Institutes of Medicine at the University of Edinburgh in 1848 (as reflected in this letter). ODNB 5:140-141. 2. Blair, Daniel. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, London, September 23, 1845. Blair writes, "I have again returned to London on my way to Southampton, from whence I sail to the West Indies on the 1st of next month. Previous to my departure I am anxious to obtain a good microscope and introduction to its application to medical purposes. I would, therefore, with your permission, put myself under your able tuition during the short time that remains for my residence in this country." Daniel Blair (1814-1857) trained in medicine in Dublin and Edinburgh before moving to British Guiana in 1834. He served as Surgeon-General of British Guiana and published a classic book on yellow fever in the West Indies. It is likely that he brought the first microscope to that part of the world. 3. Bowerbank, James Scott. Autograph Note Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, London, August 16, 1846. Bowerbank writes, "Prof. Retzius dines with me next Thursday at 5 o'clock... will you favor me with your complement to meet him?" James Scott Bowerbank (1797-1877) developed an early interest in botany, geology, and microscopy. This letter was written in his home Highbury Grove, which "became celebrated as a scientific centre in London." ODNB 6:924-925. The letter to Quekett about having dinner with Anders Adolf Retzius (1796-1860) links three European pioneers of microscopy. ODNB 45:669-670 and DSB 11:379-383. 4. Cooper, Bransby Blake. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, August 23, 1844. Cooper writes, "I fear you have forgotten me, when am I to see the phenomenon attendant on inflammation in the frog's web as promised by you." Bransby Blake Cooper (1792-1853), who was Sir Astley Cooper's nephew, taught anatomy and practiced surgery at Guy's Hospital. Plarr 1:268-270. 5. Crosse, John G. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett. Norwich, August 14, 1846. 1p. Crosse writes, in part, "I have made every arrangement in hope of seeing you & hope I shall hear by early post when I may expect you. I beg you to come directly to my house where I shall have a bed for you. At 5 on Tuesday & Wednesday I shall have many gentlemen & shall keep a place at my table for you on both days - if I learn that I may expect you." John G. Crosse (1790-1850) studied at St. George's Hospital "and at the Great Windmill Street school of anatomy, where he was noted for his skill in dissection." He published a book in 1815 that described his experiences in the teaching hospitals of Paris and later that year settled in Norwich, where "he soon gained a large practice as a surgeon." ODNB 14:437-438. 6. Curling, Thomas Blizard. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, London, March 2, 1846. 1 page. Curling thanks Quekett for sending "a share of the duplicate calculi which are to be given away." Thomas Blizard Curling (1811-1888) "was the first accurately to note the clinical picture of cretinism, which Ord was later to name 'myxedema'. Curling was also the first to suggest deficiency of the thyroid as a cause of cretinism." See Garrison-Morton-Norman 3445 and 3818. 7. Guthrie, George James. Autograph Note Signed to John Quekett, 2 p, n.p., n.d. With an engraved portrait by John Cochran (1840). Guthrie asks the microscopist to study calculi he is sending. George James Guthrie (1785-1856) "was the leading British military surgeon of the first half of the nineteenth century." ODNB 24:305-307. 8. Kiernan, Francis. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p London, February 18, 1845. Kiernan writes, "My dear Sir, I have not received the card for Mr. [Charles Chandler] Egerton and his friend and I fear you may have forgotten it. If you will send it to him at No. 1 Temple Street, White Friars, you will much oblige." Francis Kiernan (1800-1874) was a London anatomist and physician who trained at St. Bartholomew's Hospital who was elected a fellow of the Royal Society in 1834. A lecturer in anatomy and physiology at the University of London, he was elected a fellow in the Royal College of Surgeons in 1834. Plarr I:661-662.9. 9. Lawrence, Sir William. Autograph Letter Signed to John Thomas Quekett, 1 p, London, May 7, 1845. With a portrait engraved by John Cochran (1840). Lawrence writes, "Will you favor me with your company to dinner at Ealing Park on Sunday next, when I hope to see Mr. Corte (?) & a few other friends. I shall be glad to see you as early as you can come, if you are inclined to see the garden & plants & to enjoy the country. We shall dine at six." Sir William Lawrence (1783-1867) was apprenticed to John Abernethy before being elected assistant surgeon to St. Bartholomew's Hospital in 1813 and surgeon to the London Infirmary for Diseases of the Eye two years later. Lawrence served as president of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1846 and 1855. He became Serjeant-Surgeon to Queen Victoria in 1858. He practiced and taught at St. Bartholomew's Hospital for four decades. Lawrence's lectures and writings created controversy, especially when he delved into political and religious topics. "Throughout the nineteenth century, he was often regarded as a martyr for the cause of science and of intellectual liberty. His lectures were even cited a precursors for such later works of scientific naturalism as Charles Darwin's Descent of Man (1871) and Thomas Huxley's Man's Place in Nature (1865)." ODNB 32:874-876. DMB 3:776. Plarr 1:689-692. 10. Pickford, James H. Autograph Letter Signed to John T. Quekett. Brighton, 4 pp, November 11 [1845]. Pickford writes, in part, "The bones of the daughter of William the Conqueror have lately been discovered near this place & the tutor of the Parish & others are desirous that they be preserved from further decay - as it is intended to reinter them. They are in a high state of preservation - are very firm & hard - & when broken are ? white. Mr. John Adams, who has been staying with me for a day or two & who has seen the bones suggested to me that if I wrote to you on the subject you would oblige me by informing me at your earliest convenience how they should be treated in order to prevent their further decay - or falling to pieces. Adams thinks that they should be dipped in linseed oil - boiled, or not boiled - but as he is not sure about it he wishes me to write to you." James H. Pickford (1805-1875), a surgeon trained in London and Paris, practiced at Brighton until his death. The bones of William the Conqueror's fifth daughter Gundfreda were discovered in a lead chest uncovered by workmen laying the bed for the new Brighton and Hastings railway near Lewes. They hit the chest about two feet below the surface. She had died in 1085, and a headline read "Finding of the remains of the daughter of William the Conqueror and her Lord." The discovery and Pickford's role is discussed in the Illustrated London News (November 8, 1845, p. 295). 11. Todd, Robert Bentley. Autograph Letter Signed to John Quekett, 1 p, London, July 17, 1849. Todd writes, in part, "Will you give the bearer, Dr. Davies of Bath, the opportunity of seeing your collection of microscopic preparations." Robert Bentley Todd (1809-1860) was born in Ireland but spent his career in London beginning in 1830. "Todd appreciated that the improvements in the microscope made in the 1820s provided the technology to move beyond the gross anatomy of the early physiologists. He accurately predicted that microscopic anatomy and organic chemistry, accompanied by careful observation of symptoms during life, would form the basis for future medical progress." ODNB 54:884-887. 12. Pattison, Granville Sharp. Autograph Letter Signed to John's older brother Edwin John Quekett, 1 p, London, March 28, 1827. With a small (clipped) admission ticket for Quekett signed by Pattison. Pattison writes, "I send you on the other side an order of admission to my lectures to be delivered on the evening of Friday next at the Royal Institution at a little before 9 o'clock. Should your father feel disposed to attend I shall be most happy to see him. Have the kindness to send my compliments to the ladies." 13. Thomson, Anthony Todd. Autograph Document Signed, being a testimonial for John's older brother Edwin John Quekett, 1 p, University of London, April 12, 1832. Thomson writes, in part, "These are to certify that Mr. Edwin J. Quickett [sic] was a pupil of mine, in the class of Materia Medica and Therapeutics, in this University; and distinguished himself as a very attentive student, eager for information, and not failing to seize every opportunity of acquiring it.... He is, in every respect, well informed in his profession; and, with a mind much above the common standard, is fully adequate to take charge of any Medical Institution to which he may be appointed. Indeed I conceive that any Medical Charity must flourish under his superintendence, Anthony Todd Thomson, MD." Anthony Todd Thomson (1778-1849) was a very successful London physician who "gained a reputation for the care and attention he bestowed on patients.... In 1828 he was appointed the first professor of materia medica and therapeutics at the newly founded London University." ODNB 54:489-490. 14. Davis, Thomas. Autograph Letter Signed [recommendation for] Edwin John Quekett, 1 p, London, July 28, 1834. Davis writes, "It gives me much pleasure to have an opportunity of expressing the high sense I entertain of Mr. Quekett's medical & general scientific acquirements; his education, his ability & moral character most fully qualify him for the practice of his profession. Thomas Davis, M.D., Lecturer on Medicine & Physician to the London Hospital." Thomas Davis (1778-1863) was elected a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons the year he wrote this letter. Plarr I:326. John Thomas Quekett was a pioneer of English microscopy and a leading microscopist of his generation. He gained an interest in natural history from his father and learned medicine as an apprentice to his older brother Edwin John Quekett (1808-1847). "He entered King's College and worked at the London Hospital medical school, qualifying at Apothecaries' Hall and the Royal College of Surgeons in 1840. He won a competitive three-year studentship in human and comparative anatomy at the latter in the same year, and on its completion in 1843 was appointed assistant conservator to the Hunterian Museum of the College of Surgeons, under Richard Owen, becoming demonstrator of minute anatomy in 1844.... In 1841, on Owen's recommendation, he had been appointed secretary of the recently founded Microscopical Society of London. He retained the post until 1860, when he became president.... Quekett's work as a histologist, both practical and literary, was original and prolific. His Practical Treatise on the Use of the Microscope (1848) was the first such work, and gave much encouragement to individual workers at this fruitful time in the use of the instrument in histology. He was a well-connected man of considerable scientific stature (the prince consort was among those who came to him for instruction). He was working with the microscope during the period in which it was becoming established as a serious scientific tool." ODNB 45:669-670. The Microscopical Society had been founded in 1839 in the house of his brother Edwin. In 1865, four years after John Quekett's death, the Quekett Microscopical Club was formed in London with Edwin Lankester as its first president. With Gerard L'E. Turner. Micrographia Historica: The Study of the History of the Microscope. Quekett Lecture. Oxford 1972,, stiff wrappers. With a frontispiece portrait of Quekett and with Turner's visiting card laid in. Edwin John Quekett (1808-1847) was a surgeon and microscopist who became a member of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1830 and was appointed lecturer on botany at London Hospital in 1835. "He was elected a fellow of the Linnean Society in 1836. A meeting, held at his house in 1839, resulted in the foundation of the Microscopical Society of London (later the Royal Microscopical Society), which was to exert so great an influence on the development of the instrument" (ODNB 45:670). Granville Sharp Pattison (1792-1851) was a Scottish-born anatomist who came to America in 1818 and was professor of anatomy, physiology and surgery at the University of Maryland from 1820 to 1825. He returned to England in 1826, where he "for a short time occupied the important post of professor of anatomy at the University of London" (Kelly Burrage 950-951). In 1831 he returned to America where he would become professor at Jefferson Medical College. Pattison was "one of the most successful teachers of anatomy in the first half of the nineteenth century" (DAMB 2:584-585). This admission ticket was presented to Edwin John Quekett (1808-1847) when he was just embarking on a career as a surgeon and pioneering English microscopist. "He underwent training at University College Hospital, becoming a member of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1830....A meeting, held in his house in 1839, resulted in the foundation of the Microscopical Society of London (later the Royal Microscopical Society), which was to exert so great an influence on the development of the instrument" (ODNB 45:670). Joseph Jackson Lister was among the group of anatomists, botanists, entomologists, and zoologists who attended the organizational meeting.

title: MEDICAL PHOTOGRAPHY. CHEEVER, DAVID. and J. NELSON BORLAND. 2 works:
description: MEDICAL PHOTOGRAPHY. CHEEVER, DAVID. and J. NELSON BORLAND. 2 works: 1. First Medical And Surgical Report Of The Boston City Hospital . Boston: 1870. Marginal stain affecting 13 leaves. Otherwise very fine. First edition. David Cheever's article "On Excisions of Joints" is illustrated with two mounted photographs of a young girl who had undergone excision of the head of her femur. This is a very early example of the use of photography to document surgical results. Citing this volume, surgical historian Ira Rutkow writes, "Cheever's work is important because of its early use of photographs. The wet process of making albumen photographs was time-consuming and required mounting actual photographs by hand. Two such photographs are part of an article by Cheever on excision of joints (pages 71-107)" (Rutkow, The History of Surgery in the United States 1775-1900. Volume 1, San Francisco 1988, GS69). Rowley, Photo Illustrated Medical Literature 22, incorrectly states that there are 3 photographs rather than 2. This thick volume also contains reports by several prominent Boston physicians and surgeons, such as Henry I. Bowditch, Howard Damon (on dermatology), and Henry Williams (on ophthalmology). 2. CHEEVER, DAVID. "On Excision of the Elbow Joint." IN: Medical and Surgical Reports of the Boston City Hospital. Second Series , pp 143-149, plus 6 inserted leaves of heliotype photographs, Boston 1877. Large folding frontispiece illustration of the Boston City Hospital. Publisher's cloth-backed printed paper-covered boards, Fine. First edition. The photographs depict the bones removed from the first patient, a picture of him with his arm outstretched after recovery, two photographs of the excised "new joint" that was photographed when the first patient died six years after the operation, and two photographs of the second patient, one with the arm at rest and the other with the arm in action. Cheever had been appointed surgeon to the Boston City Hospital in 1870. Kelly Burrage 217-219.

description: KELLY, HOWARD A. 1858-1943. "Report in Gynecology I. 1890," IN: Johns Hopkins Hospital Reports, Volume 2, numbers 3-4, pp 1-122, 2 photographic plates. Removed from bound volume, some light spotting and even toning. FIRST EDITION . This report includes 15 articles by Howard A. Kelly, the first Gynecologist-in-Chief of the Johns Hopkins Hospital and one of the "Four Doctors" in John Singer Sargent's famous painting. Kelly opens his report by declaring, "Show me a man's operating room, and I will tell you the character of his work." The two photographs by Philadelphia photographer Frederick Gutekunst depict Kelly's operating room with its elaborate state-of-the-art apparatus for performing aseptic surgery. Gutekunst (1831-1917) has been described as the "dean of American photographers" (John Hannavy, Encyclopedia of Nineteenth Century Photography, 2007, 1:629).

description: HAMILTON, ALICE. 1869-1970. 5 Offprints: 1. "The Clinical Course And Pathological Histology Of A Case Of Neuroglioma Of The Brain" (coauthored with Henry Thomas as first author), 1897. Printed wrappers. Slight chipping to spine, wrappers slightly soiled and browned. 2. "Multiple Tuberculous Ulcers of the Stomach, with a Report of Three Cases," 1897. Self-wrappers. Toning, a few finger marks. 3. "On the Presence of New Elastic Fibres in Tumors," 1900. Printed wrappers. Slight chipping to spine edge, wrappers toned. 4. "Surgical Scarlatina," 1904. Printed blue wrappers. Some soiling to wrappers. 5. "The Question of Virulence Among the So-Called Pseudodiphtheria Bacilli," 1904. Printed wrappers. Toning. Offprints 4 and 5 bear gynecologist and pathologist Thomas Cullen's name stamp. Alice Hamilton was a pioneer of industrial medicine who received her medical degree from the University of Michigan and did postgraduate work in Germany and at Johns Hopkins. These publications reflect her plan of a career in pathology and bacteriology. The first three papers were published in 1897, the year she took her first job in the pathology department at the Women's Medical College of Northwestern University. "During the years she taught at Northwestern, she lived at Hull House in Chicago, where she started a well-baby clinic. Her concern with social and humanitarian issues matured, due in part to experiences while she resided in Hull House. Jane Adams, Florence Kelly, and Julia Lathrop influenced Hamilton, and the experience of living close to working people who suffered from injustice, poverty, and disease affected her social conscience.... It is generally acknowledged, on the basis of her contributions to occupational medicine alone, that Hamilton was an outstanding woman of her generation. However, if one considers her involvements with social issues, her status increases to an even greater degree" (Jacqueline Corn in ANB 9:910-912). These offprints provide insight into Hamilton's professional activities as a teacher and researcher of pathology at the earliest stage of her career.

William Stewart Halsted was a "world-famous surgeon, clinical teacher, and member of the Johns Hopkins 'Big Four' who left an indelible impress upon an entire generation of American surgeons. He combined experimental work in physiology and pathology with innovative surgical techniques; originated the procedure of 'blood refusion' for carbonic oxide poisoning; pioneered the use of cocaine for local anesthesia; introduced a host of new surgical techniques and procedures dealing with cancers, hernias, goiters, and aneurysms; was an early proponent of aseptic surgery; and emphasized the need for careful exacting procedures in the operating room. Over and above his skill and originality in surgery, Halsted made significant physiological and clinical studies of cancer, thyroid and parathyroids, blood vessels and other subjects." John Duffy. Dictionary of American Medical Biography, 320. Clinician-historian Kenneth Ludmerer describes Halsted as "America's greatest surgeon." Halsted did not publish any books. This collection of Halsted's offprints is remarkable for its comprehensiveness and condition. Three of the books are association copies. Alfred Blalock (1899-1964) was the third surgeon-in-chief of the Johns Hopkins Hospital. His best known contribution is his role in developing the Blalock-Taussig "Blue Baby" operation with Helen Taussig and Vivien Thomas. Philip Bard (1898-1977) was director of the Department of Physiology at Johns Hopkins from 1933 until 1961.

"Johann Friedrich Theodor 'Fritz' Muller (1821-1897), the first German to support Darwin, studied the development of Crustacea in Brazil and published some of his results in the above little book, which contains much original information. He realized the bearing of individual development on the theory of evolution" (Garrison-Morton-Norman 221). "His book, Für Darwin (1864), was a fundamental contribution to evolutionary biology at a critical moment during its infancy, and his name has been immortalized in scientific literature with the term 'Mullerian mimicry'" (McKinney in DSB IX:559-561). Christopher Johnston (1822-1891) was a University of Maryland medical graduate who studied in Europe in the 1850s. When this pamphlet was published, Johnston was professor of anatomy and physiology at his alma mater. Kelly Burrage 666-667.

description: ANESTHESIA PIONEERS. HAYWARD, GEORGE. 1791-1863. Surgical Reports, and Miscellaneous Papers on Medical Subjects. Boston: 1855. 8vo. Publisher's brown cloth. Rubbed, light toning and soiling. FIRST EDITION With clipped signature of Hayward tipped to free front endpaper. Includes Garrison-Morton-Norman 6030 among the 22 articles included in this volume. Hayward "devoted himself largely to surgical work and was known as a careful and judicious operator, so that in 1835, when Harvard established a professorship of the principles of surgery and clinical surgery, he was chosen to fill the chair. He held teaching clinics at the Massachusetts General Hospital, where he was visiting surgeon, and it was he who did the second surgical operation ever done upon a patient under the influence of ether, the removal of a fatty tumor of the shoulder on October 17, 1846 ... the day following the first operation under ether by John C. Warren. On November 7, 1846, Hayward did the first major operation under ether anesthesia in the same institution, amputation of the thigh.... The operation was done before a large audience of students and physicians, and the patient, a delicate girl of twenty, with a scrofulous knee-joint, was entirely ignorant that her leg had been removed" (Kelly Burrage 547). John Shaw Billings praised Hayward: "It is to Warren, Hayward, and Bigelow that the surgical world is indebted mainly for a sufficient, general and safe method of anaesthesia" (Billings, The History and Literature of Surgery 126). Rutkow GS35.

description: ANESTHESIA PIONEERS. CHANNING, WALTER. 1786-1876. Autograph Letter Signed, to John T. McCoun, 1 p, Boston, January 7, 1861, on half sheet of ruled paper. Channing writes: " Your favor of Dec. 11 is before me, and but for many hindrances should have been before answered. My late brother, Rev. Dr. William Ellery Channing died Oct 2nd 1841 in Bennington, Vt., while on a return journey from Lennox, Mass, where he had passed the summer. I have selected from many letters his autograph, and only regret it was so hastily written. But my brother from habit wrote very fast, and the one sent is a fair specimen of his penmanship. Very truly yrs. Walter Channing, M.D. " A few light stains. Walter Channing received his medical degree from the University of Pennsylvania where he studied under Benjamin Rush. He was the first professor of obstetrics at the Harvard Medical School. "In addition to an extensive private practice he was for nearly twenty years on the visiting staff of the Massachusetts General Hospital. Soon after the introduction of anesthetics there in 1846, he became deeply interested in the use of ether in childbirth, and mainly through his influence it was successfully used in such cases in this country.... He was a Unitarian and a great admirer of his brother, William Ellery Channing, the clergyman, and a joke which he made in connection with him has appeared in various papers even to the present time. Someone calling at his house asked for Dr. Channing and on hearing the inquiry the doctor said, 'Which Dr. Channing? My brother preaches and I practice'" (Kelly Burrage 209-300). See also Kass, Midwifery and Medicine in Boston: Walter Channing, M.D. 1786-1876, pp 168-186. John T. McCoun (1803-1861) was a prominent citizen of Troy, New York, who was president of the Farmer's Bank in that city when he corresponded with Channing. He died a few months after receiving Channing's letter.

title: ANATOMY, LEGAL ASPECTS. A group of 6 items:
description: ANATOMY, LEGAL ASPECTS. A group of 6 items: 1. BIGELOW, HENRY J. 1818-1890. Autograph Letter Signed to Levi Lincoln. 3 pp, Boston, October 9, 1859. Bigelow writes: " I endeavored in our conversation a few days ago, to explain to you our difficulty. I am loath to trespass on your valuable time, or on that of the Governor, and have endeavored in doing so to be concise. It would seem desirable to give these local authorities a hint that the Anatomy law is not a dead letter, dependent for its administration on the good will alone of a superintendent, who, if conciliated, may supply a friend or any important applicant; - and it seems also very desirable to infuse a little courage into some of these incumbents, who sometimes have, as I must think, a feeling that they are endangering their places, by meddling in a matter, which though legal, is not usually ventilated at court. The truth is that Bridgewater could probably furnish a very fair supply of subjects, from the wholly friendless 'Kanaka' sailors of New Bedford, who die there of phthisis. We cannot remonstrate with nor urge the autocrats of these institutions, as every South Sea savage would then forthwith have friends, who would request his burial. Our policy is, therefore, for obvious reasons, wholly conciliatory; and in this view my present letter to Gov. Banks might be suicidal* to our school, except that I have full confidence, in his good judgment as to the propriety of moving at all, in the matter; and especially in his great ability to determine the most judicious move to make. With many thanks for your civility.... [P.S. "*This is also the reason I have not specified in the letter [to Governor Banks] , the fact that subjects are sent out of the state - but have only alluded to it ." Henry J. Bigelow was an 1841 Harvard medical graduate who "became the leading surgeon of New England during his lifetime....and one of the pioneers in the study of surgical pathology, being one of the earliest microscopists in the country....He was elected professor of surgery at Harvard in 1849, holding this position until 1882." (Kelly Burrage, pp 95-97.) Levi Lincoln (1782-1868) was a Harvard College graduate who served as governor of Massachusetts from 1825 to 1834, when he was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, serving until 1841. "Between 1849 and 1868 Lincoln devoted himself to philanthropic, charitable, and community affairs.... Lincoln was a stable and highly respected public official during a politically chaotic time." (ANB 13:678-679.) Fold creases, browning. 2. ---. Autograph Letter Signed to Nathaniel Prentiss Banks. 4 pp, Boston, October 9, 1859. In this long letter Bigelow writes, in part: " Sir, I take the liberty respectfully to call your attention to one or two points connected with the administration of the present Anatomy law; a delicate subject concerning which it has occurred to me that a word or two from yourself, should your judgment dictate it, would greatly subserve the interests of medical education.... Last year, at the opening of the winter course of lectures here, (Nov. 1st) a period when students, by their robust health, are best prepared to encounter the fatigues of dissection, and when subjects are on that account, by far the most needed, no subject was to be had for some time. Afterwards they were procured. It is well understood that one great object of country students in attending lectures in cities, is the facility there afforded for the pursuit of this essential branch of medical education. In New York the illegal supply is generally abundant, often prodigal, but in this state where the illegal procuring of subjects is now unheard of, the working of the legal enactment is sometimes very uncertain and the law, which if enforced and carried out as was designed, would furnish an ample provision, is sometimes greatly restricted in its operation by the sort of local influences, to which I have ventured briefly to avert. I leave this subject without further suggestion, fully aware that your excellency will determine its bearings, and the general propriety or expediency of any action in relation to it, better than I should be able to do. " Nathaniel Prentiss Banks (1816-1894) was elected to the U.S. Congress in 1848 and resigned in 1857 when he became governor of Massachusetts. Abraham Lincoln appointed him Major General in the Union Troops in 1861. "During the 1820s the problem [of an inadequate supply of cadavers that were acquired legally] was agitated quite extensively before the public. A movement to legalize the supply of anatomical subjects was advancing contemporaneously in Great Britain....In this atmosphere, following a riot in New Haven in 1824, Connecticut authorized the delivery of unclaimed bodies of convicts dying in Newgate to the medical institution at Yale....Later in the decade, however, Massachusetts took the lead in this movement....As a result of this agitation the Massachusetts General Court in 1831 passes America's first real anatomy act." John Blake, "The Development of American Anatomy Acts," Journal of Medical Education. 1955. 30:431-439. Fold creases, browning. 3. Address to the Community, on the Necessity of Legalizing the Study of Anatomy. Boston: Perkins & Marvin 1829. Pamphlet (27 pp). Disbound, removed from a bound volume. WORTHINGTON HOOKER'S COPY (signature on title page). FIRST EDITION . The committee that published this pamphlet included George C. Shattuck and John C. Warren, who played a major role in securing passage of the Massachusetts Anatomy Act of 1831. In 1846 Warren performed the first major operation under ether anesthesia, which Henry J. Bigelow announced to the world through his article in the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal. Worthington Hooker (1806-1867) was an 1829 medical graduate of Harvard who became a leading physician and medical teacher of his generation. Scattered foxing. 4. DRAPER, JOHN W. 1811-1882. Petition of the Medical Faculty of the University of New York, to the Honorable the Senate and Assembly of the State of New York, for the Legalization of Anatomy. Also, an Introductory Lecture, Delivered at the Opening of the Medical Department of the University, for Session 1853-4, and Entitled an Appeal to the People of the State of New York, to Legalize the Dissection of the Dead. New York: 1854. Pamphlet. Printed wrappers. FIRST EDITION . John W. Draper received his medical degree at the University of Pennsylvania in 1836, and accepted the chair of chemistry at the University of the City of New York three years later. He co-founded the medical school at that institution in 1841. In 1850 he became Professor of Physiology and President at the Medical College. Light wear and browning. 5. "On the Importance of the Study of Anatomy." Boston: Wells & Lilly, 1825. Pamphlet (12 pp). Self-wrappers. Small library stamp on front wrapper. SIGNATURE OF REVEREND JOHN ANDREWS ON TITLE PAGE . FIRST EDITION The final lines in this pamphlet read, "The number of medical students in Boston the last season was about one hundred and thirty. If anatomy could not be learnt at home more than one hundred of these students would remain ignorant, for want of means to go to foreign countries. What miseries would their ignorance produce?" Library markings, light chipping to edges, scattered browning. 6. BLAKE, JOHN. "The Development of American Anatomy Acts." 1955. Offprint. Wrappers. Light toning.

title: Property of the late Alan Windsor, 1966 Velocette 499cc Venom Thruxton Frame no. RS18904 Engine no. VMT 377
description: Property of the late Alan Windsor 1966 Velocette 499cc Venom Thruxton Registration no. YBF 39D Frame no. RS18904 Engine no. VMT 377 • Matching numbers • An older restoration • Present ownership since 1984 • Only two owners in the last 50 years "Prestige machine of the pushrod range was the Venom Thruxton 500. It incorporated all the accumulated experience gained in the years the Venom Clubman has been raced in long-distance events, plus the development of the 12 and 24-hour record breaker." – C E A 'Titch' Allen, The Velocette Saga. Production race successes, notably in the Thruxton 500 Mile event prompted Veloce Ltd to adopt that name for their newly introduced top-of-the-range sports roadster in 1964. Based on the existing Venom, the Thruxton featured a tuned engine with revised big-valve cylinder head, Amal GP carburettor, clip-on handlebars, rear-set footrests and a twin-leading-shoe front brake as standard equipment. Although the Thruxton took its name from the eponymous Hampshire racing circuit, arguably its finest hour came in 1967 when Manxman Neil Kelly won the '500' class in the Isle of Man TT's Production race, newly introduced for that year. Although much admired by the café racing fraternity, the Thruxton's necessarily high price limited its appeal to a select handful of wealthy connoisseurs. It is estimated that as few as 1,100 were made by the factory (with a further 55-60 assembled from parts by main dealers) and today the Thruxton is one of the most sought after of post-war Velocettes. Alan Windsor purchased this example in November 1984 from Mr John Alfred Lee of Suffolk, its owner since 1972. A letter on file from the Velocette Thruxton Machine Register states that 'YBF 39D' was dispatched from the factory on 24th June 1966 to the Boult dealership in Stafford and sold new a couple of months later to a Mr Wynne. Alan had the engine and clutch professionally rebuilt in June 1988, though it is not known by whom (see details on file). Further maintenance works were carried out in December 2014 by a Velocette specialist. The machine is offered with sundry bills; some old MoTs (most recent expired September 2006); SORN paperwork; a parts list; an old-style V5 document; old/current current V5Cs; and an owner's handbook. Re-commissioning to a greater or lesser extent will be required before returning it to the road. Offered without key

description: Property of Various Owners DOSTOEVSKY CARTE-DE-VISITE INSCRIBED TO ALEXANDER HERZEN. DOSTOEVSKY, FYODOR. 1821-1881. Photograph signed and inscribed [in Russian] to Alexander Herzen, albumen print carte-de-visite full length portrait by M.B. Tulinov, Petersburg, 1861, 105 x 65 mm, inscribed by Dostoevsky in Russian to the verso, " Alexander Ivanovich Herzen in memory of our meeting in London. Fyodor Dostoyevsky 8 July/20 July 1862, " minor stain to verso. Provenance: Alexander Ivanovich Herzen; to daughter Olga Aleksandrovna [Herzen] Monod; by descent. Publication: For a discussion of the photograph, see Volgin, Igor. "Introduction" to The Dostoevsky Archive (1997), p 21. Pull quote: "Herzen awaits his readers in the future. Far above the heads of the present crowd, he transmits his thoughts to those who will be able to comprehend them." – Leo Tolstoy, 1905. VERY RARE CARTE DE VISITE PHOTOGRAPH OF FYODOR DOSTOEVSKY PRESENTED TO ALEXANDER HERZEN IN REMEMBRANCE OF THEIR 1862 MEETING IN LONDON: A TREMENDOUSLY IMPORTANT ASSOCIATION BETWEEN TWO OF THE LEADING INTELLECTUALS OF THE 19TH-CENTURY. Alexander Herzen was one of the most important and influential Russian writers and thinkers of the 19th-century. called the "father of Russian socialism," he had a profound influence on late-19th century Russian writers, including Fyodor Dostoevsky. Born illegitimately to a wealthy Russian landowner, Herzen became a dissident and critic of the Russian feudal system. Of Herzen, Tolstoy said he had never met a man "with so rare a combination of scintillating brilliance and depth." His writings, including From the Other Shore (1848) and those appearing in his influential publications of the 1850s-60s The Bell and the Polestar, would help mold a generation of Russian writing and thought. Herzen and Dostoevsky met for the first time in Russia in 1846, following Dostoevsky's comment in a letter to his brother that Herzen and Goncharov stand as "the most remarkable" of his rivals; Herzen's recollection of the meeting was less than effusive, however: "I can't say he made a particularly present impression." Their second meeting occurred when Dostoevsky visited Herzen in London in July of 1862, of which this photograph is a memento. During the 1850s and early 1860s, visits to the emigree Herzen by Russian writers and intellectuals were something of a right of passage, and Dostoevsky's visit followed right on the heels of Turgenev. This series of meetings profoundly affected Dostoevsky and his work, and is clearly acknowledged in his Winter Notes which he wrote later that year, exhibiting a clear debt to Herzen's own writings. Dostoevsky, along with Solzhenitsyn, acknowledged the formative influence of Herzen on his work, and Herzen would also appear in composite in a number of Dostoevsky's characters throughout his career. Herzen, however, noted, rather condescendingly, "Dostoevsky was here yesterday—he is a naïve, not entirely lucid, but a very dear person. He believes enthusiastically in the Russian people." The two towering figures would meet again on a steamship from Naples to Livorno the following year, where Dostoevsky was travelling with his mistress Polina Suslova. According to Suslova's diaries (as published in The Dostoevsky Archives ), Dostoevsky took pains to hide their relationship from Herzen, introducing her vaguely as a family member, and even encouraged her to arrange a visit with Herzen's son in Paris that Winter. After they parted, Dostoevsky became angry with her over a photograph of her he had seen at Herzen's, which she had given at an earlier date. In 1865, Dostoevsky wrote to Herzen imploring him for a loan, and became peevish when Herzen did not immediately respond. By the late 1860s Dostoevsky would disparage Herzen, somewhat unfairly, as a "Westernizer," leading to his more severe criticism of Herzen in his Writer's Diary. Herzen was one of the most complex and brilliant figures of the 19th-century, and was largely responsible for assimilating western ideas into Russian thought, while still maintaining his advocacy for the freedom of the Russian serf. In reality, the two writers/thinkers shared a great deal in their outlook: both asserted the importance of the individual, and the folly of the search for a unified teleological system, cutting against the grain of their mid-19th century contemporaries. While Herzen was embraced by Lenin, identified as the "father of Russian socialism," Herzen's socialism was a different breed, "Centralization may do a great deal for order and for various public undertakings, but it is incompatible with freedom. It easily brings a nation to the position of a well-tended flock or a pack of hounds cleverly kept in order by a huntsman." Lenin regarded Herzen's focus on freedom as a shortcoming of his bourgeois roots. During the 20th-century Russian-British philosopher Isaiah Berlin came across Herzen's writings and recognized the prescience of Herzen's thought. It was Berlin, who reestablished Herzen's influence, agreeing with and amplifying his idea that the pursuit of "a perfect society" invariably leads to blood. The present photograph was taken by Mikhail Borisovich Tulinov (1823–1889) in Petersburg in 1861. Any period photograph of Dostoevsky is rare, and moreso inscribed. We trace two inscribed photographs at auction in the last 40 years. However, we find no record of an inscribed photograph of similar substance and importance in the historical record. An incredible, and incredibly rare, Dostoevsky item tying together two of the greatest thinkers and writers of the 19th-century. REFERENCES: Kelly, Aileen. The Discovery of Chance: The Life and Thought of Alexander Herzen. 2016. Kelly, Aileen. "Irony and Utopia in Herzen and Dostoevsky: From the Other Shore and Diary of a Writer." The Russian Review , 50:4 (1991), pp 397-416. Lantz, Kenneth. The Dostoevsky Encycolpedia. 2004. Serakin, Peter. The Dostoevsky Archive: Firsthand Accounts of the Novelist from Contemporaries' Memoirs and Rare Periodicals . 1997. "If only people wanted to save themselves instead of saving the world, how much they would do for the salvation of the world and the liberation of humanity!" – Alexander Herzen, From the Other Shore, 1848.

title: 1968 Velocette Venom Thruxton Frame no. RS19383 Engine no. VMT599
description: 1968 Velocette Venom Thruxton Frame no. RS19383 Engine no. VMT599 *Landmark model *Long term ownership "Prestige machine of the pushrod range was the Venom Thruxton 500. It incorporated all the accumulated experience gained in the years the Venom Clubman has been raced in long-distance events, plus the development of the 12 and 24-hour record breaker." – C E A 'Titch' Allen, The Velocette Saga. Production race successes, notably in the Thruxton 500 Mile event prompted Veloce Ltd to adopt that name for their newly introduced top-of-the-range sports roadster in 1964. Based on the existing Venom, the Thruxton featured a tuned engine with revised big-valve cylinder head, Amal GP carburettor, clip-on handlebars, rear-set footrests and a twin-leading-shoe front brake as standard equipment. Although the Thruxton took its name from the eponymous Hampshire racing circuit, arguably its finest hour came in 1967 when Manxman Neil Kelly won the '500' class in the Isle of Man TT's Production race, newly introduced for that year. Although much admired by the café racing fraternity, the Thruxton's necessarily high price limited its appeal to a select handful of wealthy connoisseurs. It is thought that as few as 1,100 were made by the factory (with a further 55-60 assembled from parts by main dealers) and today the Thruxton is one of the most sought after of post-war Velocette's. Offered without documents, this clean example of Velocette's premier model will need recommissioning to a greater or lesser extent given it's time being on static display in the late vendors private museum. A chance to own one of the legendary production racing motorcycles from the glory years of the 1960's.

title: 1913 Hudson Model 37 Roadster Chassis no. 36709
description: 1913 Hudson Model 37 Roadster Registration no. BF 8866 Chassis no. 36709 Odometer reading: tbc MOT: Exempt *Formerly part of the Henry Petronis Collection in the USA *An older restoration *Well presented with a lovely patina In July 1912, Hudson's Model 33 range, which had included the high-performance 'Mile-A-Minute' roadster, was superseded by the longer wheelbase Model 37. The latter was powered by a four-cylinder 37hp Continental engine displacing 280.6ci (4.6 litres) and drove via a three-speed transmission with cork insert clutch. This Hudson Model 37 roadster was formerly part of the private collection belonging to Henry Petronis of Easton, Maryland, having previously spent time with Kelly Kinzle Antiques in Pennsylvania. Before that, it was in the estate of Hudson enthusiast Earl W Beck. One of five body styles in the 1913 Model 37 line-up, the roadster features a high-quality grained vinyl top with twin glass rear windows and handsome nickel-plated brightwork, while the leather trimmed dashboard has all the correct, and rare, instruments and switches. The car appears to be an older and sympathetic restoration of what was clearly a well-preserved example. The round fuel tank is likely not original: probably fitted to give the car more of the 'Mile-A-Minute' look. Originally, it had a turtle deck that matched the cowl in shape. The enthusiast vendor purchased the Hudson from Bonhams' sale at the Philadelphia Simeone Foundation Automotive Museum in October 2018 (Lot 130), at which time it was reported to be in running condition following a recent service and the fitting of new tyres. Apart from a few VCC events, the Hudson has seen little use since importation. Offering the prospect of considerable performance at an 'entry-level' price, this rare 'Edwardian' roadster comes with a V5C document.

title: A costume continuity file for Grace Kelly and cast members of Rear Window
description: Property of Various Owners A costume continuity file for Grace Kelly and cast members of Rear Window Paramount Pictures, 1954. Comprising five 4 x 5 in. wardrobe test photographs of Grace Kelly, with 2 pages of notes regarding her costumes; a 4 x 5 in. wardrobe photo of Thelma Ritter with 2 pages of notes; eight 4 x 5 in. photos of Georgine Darcy (Miss Torso) with 4 pages of notes; and thirty-two 4 x 5 in. photos of the remainder of the female cast, whose characters' names are written on the top right of each page including Miss Lonely Hearts, Miss Hearing Aid, Fire Escape Woman, and more. The notes for each costume detail color, fabric, corresponding jewelry and accessories, and more, and seem to be written by several different people, though " H. Coleman " is noted as the assistant at the top of each page. Costume designer Edith Head considered Grace Kelly the perfect clotheshorse. Slim and elegant, she looked good in everything. Nevertheless, Head did avoid bright colors and loud prints for Kelly. The designs she created for Kelly's role as fashion model Lisa Fremont in Rear Window follow the path of the character's transformation from conservative model to confident adventuress. Photos: 4 x 5 in.

title: An Alfred Hitchcock large photographic archive from Rear Window
description: Property of Various Owners An Alfred Hitchcock large photographic archive from Rear Window Paramount Pictures, 1954. Comprising approximately 166 silver gelatin photographs, the majority of which are 8 x 10 in., with one signed ("Raymond Burr"); an 8 x 10 in. color transparency; two 4 x 5 in. color transparencies; and two 4 x 5 in. black-and-white candid shots. Many of the photos are doubleweight keybook stills, and many have informational snipes and stamps on the reverse. Photographer represented and/or attributed to is Bud Fraker. When the massive and murderous Raymond Burr catches Grace Kelly prowling in his apartment, the tone is set for suspense in Hitchcock's masterpiece starring Jimmy Stewart. Stewart plays a temporarily immobile photographer whose boredom at home leads him to spy on his neighbors with a telephoto lens. His curiosity puts both his life and that of his love interest, Kelly, in danger. This comprehensive archive features photos of Hitchcock directing, Kelly and Stewart clowning on the set, behind-the-scenes filming, several candid shots of Jimmy Stewart with his family during the time he was filming Rear Window , scene stills, portraits of the other cast members including Raymond Burr, Thelma Ritter, Georgine Darcy, and Wendell Corey, glamour and candid portraits of Kelly, and much more. 8 x 10 in. and smaller

title: 1966 Velocette 499cc Venom Thruxton Frame no. RS18824 Engine no. VMT 336
description: 1966 Velocette 499cc Venom Thruxton Registration no. EUG 12D Frame no. RS18824 Engine no. VMT 336 • Full matching numbers: frame, engine, registration • Fully restored in 2010 • Highly original "Prestige machine of the pushrod range was the Venom Thruxton 500. It incorporated all the accumulated experience gained in the years the Venom Clubman has been raced in long-distance events, plus the development of the 12 and 24-hour record breaker." – C E A 'Titch' Allen, The Velocette Saga. Production race successes, notably in the Thruxton 500 Mile event prompted Veloce Ltd to adopt that name for their newly introduced top-of-the-range sports roadster in 1964. Based on the existing Venom, the Thruxton featured a tuned engine with revised big-valve cylinder head, Amal GP carburettor, clip-on handlebars, rear-set footrests and a twin-leading-shoe front brake as standard equipment. Although the Thruxton took its name from the eponymous Hampshire racing circuit, arguably its finest hour came in 1967 when Manxman Neil Kelly won the '500' class in the Isle of Man TT's Production race, newly introduced for that year. Although much admired by the café racing fraternity, the Thruxton's necessarily high price limited its appeal to a select handful of wealthy connoisseurs. It is thought that as few as 1,100 were made by the factory (with a further 55-60 assembled from parts by main dealers) and today the Thruxton is one of the most sought after of post-war Velocettes. Previously forming part of a well-known collection, this genuine, early, matching-numbers Thruxton was delivered new to one of the most famous of all Velocette dealers, L Stevens Ltd of Goldhawk Road, Shepherd's Bush, London W12, on 1st April 1966 finished in silver with a blue frame. The machine has covered a mere 338 miles since a full restoration in 2010, which included an engine bottom-end rebuild by Nick Payton. Recently fettled in the present ownership, which included tuning the Amal GP carburettor, the machine is said to start easily and run and sound like it should. The Thruxton is described by the vendor as highly original, retaining correct finishes on components and fasteners (the majority of the latter are the Rubery Owen originals). Other noteworthy features include new shock absorbers (originals included); original Dunlop alloy wheel rims shod with new tyres; BTH TT magneto; original Lucas dynamo; and rebuilt Smiths instruments. Used regularly and described by the enthusiast vendor as in excellent condition, this rare and desirable Thruxton is offered with an old-style logbook, restoration invoices, dating letter, and a V5C document.

This box was given as a gift to attendees of the wedding of Frank Sinatra and Mia Farrow. Adolph Green likely first encountered Sinatra whilst working in Hollywood for M.G.M. Comden and Green wrote the screenplay and lyrics for On The Town as an adaptation of their Broadway play and Sinatra played the role of Chip alongside Gene Kelly's Gabey. Penned as a followup to On The Town and intended for Broadway, Kelly apparently got hold of the project and insisted it be made as a musical film with M.G.M. description: On The Town /Adolph Green A script for On The Town , 96 pp, mimeographed typescript, the orange paper covers inscribed, " Phyllis Newman ," with some pages annotated and amended in Adolph Green's hand, the reverse of the last page annotated in Green's hand during a flight to Los Angeles with some musings; with a bound presentation script for On The Town , presented to Adolph Green from the Screenwriters Guild, bound with a typescript presentation note: " The Screen Writer's Guild, Award to Adolph Green for his contribution to 'On The Town' the best written musical of 1949 " [cover and spine detached]; and another copy of the script, 92 pp, mimeographed typescript, with black paper covers with " Tams-Witmark Music Library Inc. " paper label, with minor annotations in pencil in Adolph Green's hand, including on the title page with notes on orchestrations; and two corresponding playbills. On The Town was penned by Adolph Green and Betty Comden after Jerome Robbins' ballet of 1944 Fancy Free with music by Leonard Bernstein. This was Comden and Green's first Broadway success and it premiered on Broadway at the Adelphi Theater, New York, on December 28, 1944. The musical featured several hit songs including New York, New York . The musical became a blockbuster Hollywood movie released in 1949 and starring Gene Kelly and Frank Sinatra. title: 1967 Velocette 499cc Venom Thruxton Frame no. RS19208 Engine no. VMT 506
description: 1967 Velocette 499cc Venom Thruxton Registration no. JOE 906E Frame no. RS19208 Engine no. VMT 506 • Motorcycle engineer owner • Cylinder head overhauled and dynamo reconditioned recently "Prestige machine of the pushrod range was the Venom Thruxton 500. It incorporated all the accumulated experience gained in the years the Venom Clubman has been raced in long-distance events, plus the development of the 12 and 24-hour record breaker." – C E A 'Titch' Allen, The Velocette Saga. Production race successes, notably in the Thruxton 500 Mile event prompted Veloce Ltd to adopt that name for their newly introduced top-of-the-range sports roadster in 1964. Based on the existing Venom, the Thruxton featured a tuned engine with revised big-valve cylinder head, Amal GP carburettor, clip-on handlebars, rear-set footrests and a twin-leading-shoe front brake as standard equipment. Although the Thruxton took its name from the eponymous Hampshire racing circuit, arguably its finest hour came in 1967 when Manxman Neil Kelly won the '500' class in the Isle of Man TT's Production race, newly introduced for that year. Although much admired by the café racing fraternity, the Thruxton's necessarily high price limited its appeal to a select handful of wealthy connoisseurs. It is thought that as few as 1,100 were made by the factory (with a further 55-60 assembled from parts by main dealers) and today the Thruxton is one of the most sought after of post-war Velocettes. Factory records show that this Thruxton was despatched from Hall Green on 28th February 1967, bound for the Colmore Depot dealership in Birmingham, and sold new to a Mr T A Needham. Formerly belonging to the noted Velocette collector, Ken Gardiner, the machine was purchased by the vendor from a deceased's estate in 2019. The current vendor is a renowned and highly capable motorcycle engineer, during whose ownership the frame has been powder coated, the cylinder head overhauled by KTT Services, and dynamo reconditioned (bills on file). The Velo was last ridden in 2012 but has been started recently and should require only minimal re-commissioning before returning to the road. Accompanying paperwork includes an old-style continuation logbook (1972), Thruxton Register dating letter, and old/current V5C documents.
